sourceContent.headline: Sleep Tech Market Size To Exceed $143.0 Billion By 2035
sourceContent.description: Sleep Tech Market growth is driven by AI-powered monitoring, smart wellness solutions, and rising awareness of sleep health worldwide.
paragraphs: The global Sleep Tech Market is entering a new phase of expansion as consumers, healthcare providers, and employers increasingly recognize quality sleep as a cornerstone of long-term health and productivity. " According to a recent study by SNS Insider, the global Sleep Tech Market size valued at USD 27.46 billion in 2025, is anticipated to grow to USD 143.0 billion by 2035, registering a CAGR of 17.96% over the 2026–2035 forecast period."

As connected health technologies, wearable devices, smart bedding systems, and AI-assisted wellness services become more popular, people are becoming more knowledgeable and aware of their sleep practice. The rise in instances of sleep dysfunction, growing awareness of health issues, and increased digital healthcare infrastructure are paving the way for investment in advanced equipment that is able to offer personalized insight while supporting preventive healthcare strategy for home and hospital environments.
To Get Detailed Insights on the Sleep Tech Market – Request a Sample Report
AI and Digital Health Revolution Reshape Sleep Management

Due to advances in artificial intelligence, the sleep technology industry is rapidly developing. Sleep technology is moving away from basic sleep tracking to provide users with practical advice. In particular, smart ecosystems that include wearable devices, environmental management systems, mobile apps and smart home technology are helping people adjust their sleeping rituals to maximize recovery.

In addition, healthcare professionals are also benefiting from new digital sleep technologies that provide remote monitoring, digital insomnia treatments and artificial intelligence-enhanced diagnostic methods. The corporate world is adding impetus to the growth of the sleep technology industry by encouraging employees to apply these technologies.

Sleep Trackers remained the leading product category, accounting for 35.42% of market revenue in 2025, supported by widespread consumer adoption of smart wearables . Meanwhile, Smart Mattresses are projected to register the fastest growth, advancing at a 19.23% CAGR through 2035 as demand rises for intelligent sleep environments.

Among technologies, Wearable Devices captured 40.33% of global revenue in 2025 due to their convenience and growing health-monitoring capabilities. AI-Enabled Solutions are expected to emerge as the fastest-growing technology segment with a 21.07% CAGR, reflecting increasing demand for predictive analytics and personalized sleep coaching.

By end user, the Residential/Household segment accounted for 48.19% of total market revenue in 2025, while Wellness & Fitness Centers are forecast to expand at the fastest pace with a 20.01% CAGR during the forecast period.

Across distribution channels, Online Retail led the market with a 38.92% revenue share in 2025, whereas Specialty Stores are anticipated to witness the highest growth, progressing at a 20.55% CAGR through 2035.

Technology firms are increasingly integrating sleep solutions into broader digital wellness ecosystems. Customers can now construct customized sleeping environments with little manual intervention thanks to AI-powered coaching platforms, non-contact monitoring sensors, connected lighting systems, automated temperature adjustment, and voice-enabled home assistants. Additionally, innovation in digital therapeutics and remote healthcare is speeding up, making it possible for doctors to monitor patients more efficiently and increase access to evidence-based sleep improvement programs. These improvements are projected to strengthen long-term consumer engagement and create recurring income opportunities across software, subscription services, and linked devices.

With the help of sophisticated healthcare infrastructure, high consumer awareness, and extensive use of digital health technology, North America continued to hold the top spot in 2025. In 2025, the United States generated USD 8.24 billion, accounting for about 85.6% of North American market revenue. The U.S. market is expected to grow at a rate of about 18% CAGR and reach about USD 42.9 billion by 2035.

Through 2035, Asia Pacific is predicted to maintain its position as the fastest-growing regional market because to increased wearable adoption, rising smartphone penetration, and rising investments in digital healthcare. In 2025, China contributed about 41.3% of regional income.

The United Kingdom accounted for 23.7% of regional revenue in Europe, the United Arab Emirates for 28.4% of the Middle East and Africa market, and Brazil for 43.2% of Latin American revenue. These figures demonstrate the increased interest of consumers in linked wellness technology.
Leading Companies Accelerate Innovation Across the Industry

Competition within the global sleep tech industry continues to intensify as companies invest in AI capabilities, biometric sensing, connected hardware, and clinically validated digital health platforms. Strategic product launches, software enhancements, and ecosystem partnerships are strengthening competitive positioning while expanding consumer adoption worldwide.

Major companies operating in the Sleep Tech Market include ResMed Inc., Philips Healthcare (Philips Respironics), Apple Inc., Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd., Garmin Ltd., Fitbit (Google), Oura Health, Eight Sleep Inc., Sleep Number Corporation, Withings SA, Dreem (ResMed), Nox Medical, SleepScore Labs, Beddr Inc., Casper Sleep Inc., Purple Innovation LLC, Tempur-Pedic, Fisher & Paykel Healthcare, Inspire Medical Systems, and SomnoMed .

An SNS Insider analyst Parry Kardani commented, "The convergence of artificial intelligence, connected health ecosystems, and growing awareness of sleep's role in overall wellness is redefining the global sleep technology industry. Companies delivering accurate monitoring, personalized recommendations, and seamless user experiences will be best positioned to capitalize on the market's strong long-term growth trajectory.

paragraphs: Consumer Products and Services News Automobiles and Parts News
Industrials and Utilities News Aerospace and Defense News

“According to BCC Research, the global livestock monitoring market is projected to grow from $5.6 billion in 2024 to $10.3 billion by 2030, at a CAGR of 10.6%, driven by increasing adoption of AI-enabled precision farming, IoT sensors, wearable technologies and growing demand for animal health, productivity and traceability.”
July 17, 2026 08:48 ET | Source: BCC Research LLC BCC Research LLC

Boston, July 17, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- The global livestock monitoring market is projected to grow from $6.2 billion in 2025 to $10.3 billion by 2030, representing a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 10.6%, according to a new report from BCC Research titled Global Livestock Monitoring Market . BCC Research is a leading provider of market intelligence and analysis for emerging technologies.

• Robust Market Expansion: The livestock monitoring market will experience strong double-digit growth at 10.6% CAGR through 2030, driven by accelerating digitization of animal agriculture and the increasing need for data-driven herd management across dairy, beef, and poultry operations. • Europe Leads Global Adoption: Europe commands the largest regional market share at 33.2%, reflecting the region's advanced agricultural infrastructure, stringent animal welfare regulations, and early adoption of precision livestock farming technologies. • Precision Farming Revolution: Growing adoption of precision livestock farming (PLF) technologies is transforming traditional farming practices, enabling producers to boost farm productivity, reduce animal mortality, and improve overall herd health while simultaneously lowering operating costs. • Protein Demand Catalyst: Rising global demand for protein is driving productivity optimization initiatives, compelling livestock producers to implement monitoring solutions that maximize output efficiency and ensure consistent supply chains. • Regulatory and Sustainability Focus: Stricter animal welfare regulations and increasing emphasis on sustainable livestock production are creating compliance-driven demand for comprehensive monitoring systems that demonstrate responsible farming practices. • Market Leadership: Key industry players driving innovation include MSD Animal Health, IDEXX Laboratories Inc., Nedap, GEA Group Aktiengesellschaft, DeLaval, Lely, BouMatic, Afimilk Ltd., DAIRYMASTER, and Fancom BV.

The livestock monitoring market's growth trajectory is underpinned by powerful structural forces reshaping modern agriculture. The digitization of animal agriculture represents a fundamental shift toward data-driven farm management, where real-time monitoring capabilities enable producers to make informed decisions about animal health, breeding optimization, and resource allocation. This technological evolution coincides with mounting pressure to increase productivity amid rising global protein consumption, particularly in developing markets where dietary shifts are driving unprecedented demand. Regulatory compliance is emerging as an equally compelling driver, with governments worldwide implementing stricter animal welfare standards and environmental sustainability requirements. These mandates are forcing producers to adopt comprehensive monitoring systems that provide verifiable data on animal treatment, health outcomes, and farming practices, creating sustained demand for advanced surveillance technologies.

The livestock monitoring market presents attractive investment opportunities for technology companies and agricultural equipment manufacturers positioned to capitalize on the sector's digital transformation. Companies developing AI-powered analytics, wearable sensors, and cloud-based management platforms are particularly well-positioned to capture market share. However, investors should consider adoption barriers including high initial capital requirements for smaller farms and connectivity limitations in rural markets. Leading players like IDEXX Laboratories, DeLaval, and GEA Group offer established market positions with proven track records, while emerging technology providers focusing on camera-based analytics and IoT sensor solutions present higher-growth potential despite execution risks.

The report provides comprehensive market sizing, segmentation analysis, competitive intelligence, and five-year forecasts for the global livestock monitoring market. Global Livestock Monitoring Market examines market dynamics across regions, technology categories, and livestock segments through 2030.

Our experienced industry analysts assess growth trends, identify and evaluate new and changing market opportunities, and provide critical information and innovative decision support tools to help inform the strategic decision-making process.

This impressive growth trajectory is primarily driven by the increasing adoption of automation and digitalization in dairy farming, as producers worldwide strive to enhance productivity, animal health, and overall operational efficiency.

The Dairy Herd Management Market is entering a transformative phase as dairy producers across the Middle East and Africa (MEA) embrace technology-driven farming practices to improve productivity, animal health, and long-term sustainability.

With rising demand for milk and dairy products, increasing urbanization, changing dietary preferences, and government initiatives supporting food security, dairy farmers are moving beyond traditional herd management methods toward intelligent, data-driven operations.

Modern dairy herd management combines advanced monitoring systems, automated feeding technologies, reproductive management tools, health monitoring devices, and cloud-based analytics into a unified ecosystem.

Instead of relying solely on manual observation, farmers now have access to real-time insights that improve decision-making, reduce operational costs, and maximize milk production.

For the Middle East and Africa, where climate challenges, water scarcity, disease outbreaks, and limited skilled labor often affect dairy operations, effective herd management has become more than a productivity tool—it has become an essential strategy for building resilient and profitable dairy businesses.

Dairy herd management refers to the systematic planning, monitoring, and optimization of every aspect of dairy cattle operations. It includes animal nutrition, breeding, reproduction, milk production, disease prevention, health monitoring, genetic improvement, housing conditions, and farm performance analysis.

Today’s dairy herd management systems integrate multiple technologies such as livestock monitoring sensors, RFID identification systems, automated milking equipment, smart feeding systems, farm management software, artificial intelligence analytics, IoT-enabled wearable devices, and cloud-based performance dashboards.

These technologies work together to provide farmers with actionable insights that improve herd efficiency while maintaining high standards of animal welfare.

Food security has become one of the highest priorities for governments across the Middle East and Africa. Heavy dependence on dairy imports has prompted countries to strengthen domestic milk production by investing in modern dairy farming.

Efficient herd management allows dairy farms to increase milk yield without significantly increasing herd size, making it an attractive solution for regions seeking greater self-sufficiency.

Population growth, increasing disposable incomes, and changing consumer lifestyles are driving higher consumption of fresh milk, cheese, yogurt, butter, and other dairy products across the region.

As consumer demand rises, commercial dairy farms are investing in technologies that ensure consistent milk quality, better animal health, and higher production efficiency.

Extreme temperatures, water shortages, and changing environmental conditions present significant challenges for dairy farmers throughout MEA.

Modern herd management technologies help address these issues by: monitoring heat stress, optimizing water consumption, improving feed efficiency, detecting health problems earlier, and reducing production losses

These capabilities are becoming increasingly valuable as climate resilience becomes central to agricultural planning.

Precision Livestock Monitoring. Wearable collars, ear tags, and activity trackers continuously monitor animal movement, feeding behaviour, rumination, body temperature, and reproductive cycles.

Rather than waiting for visible symptoms, farmers receive early alerts that enable preventive care and faster intervention.

Artificial Intelligence in Dairy Farming. Artificial intelligence is changing how dairy farms operate by analyzing large volumes of animal performance data.

AI-powered systems can: predict disease risks, detect estrus more accurately, forecast milk production, recommend feeding adjustments, improve breeding decisions, optimise labour allocation.

These predictive capabilities reduce uncertainty while increasing farm efficiency.

Automated Milking Systems. Automation is gradually gaining momentum in larger commercial dairy operations across the Middle East.

Automated milking systems provide consistent milking schedules, better milk quality, reduced labour requirements, improved animal comfort, and higher operational efficiency.

Although adoption remains limited among smaller farms, larger dairy enterprises increasingly recognize automation as a long-term investment.

Smart Feeding Technologies. Feed represents one of the largest operational expenses in dairy farming.

Smart feeding systems analyze: animal nutritional requirements, milk production levels, feed conversion efficiency, weight gain, and lactation stages.

This enables farmers to reduce feed waste while maximizing milk output.

Countries in the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) are investing heavily in advanced dairy infrastructure despite challenging climatic conditions.

sourceContent.description: Since the arrival of ChatGPT in November 2022, our world has been filled with the term 'generative AI.' paragraphs: Since the arrival of ChatGPT in November 2022, our world has been filled with the term 'generative AI.' Writing text, drawing pictures, and generating code—the AI on our screens has certainly changed the way we work.

However, the person at the center of that frenzy is now beginning to talk about the 'next wave.' That person is Jensen Huang, CEO of semiconductor giant Nvidia. He has been repeatedly mentioning a figure of '$50 trillion,' a scale that is hard to believe.

In this article, I will carefully break down what the next theme Huang calls 'Physical AI' means, analyze the components of that $50 trillion figure, and explain how individual investors should approach this wave, which is being called a 'once-in-a-decade' opportunity. Along the way, I will introduce five noteworthy Japanese stocks that are not yet widely known. I have selected stocks that offer the 'joy of discovery,' rather than household names like Toyota or Sony.

Please note that this article is not intended to recommend the buying or selling of any specific stocks, but is for informational purposes only. Please make investment decisions at your own risk. The author is not an advisor with investment advisory qualifications. Now, let's begin.
To begin with, what is 'Physical AI'?—From inside the screen to the real world

Generative AI may seem omnipotent, but it actually has a major limitation: it cannot leave the screen. Even if it can create text, images, and code, it cannot pick up a cup in front of it, carry luggage, or tighten a screw.

On the other hand, the vast majority of the world's GDP is actually generated in the 'physical world.' Making, transporting, assembling, and repairing things—these labor tasks performed by humans using their bodies are the foundation of the economy. Generative AI has barely touched this massive domain.
That is why evolving AI into an 'intelligence capable of moving in the real world' is attracting attention as the next major frontier. This is the starting point of the concept of 'Physical AI.'
Defining Physical AI—'Perception,' 'Reasoning,' and 'Action'

Simply put, Physical AI is 'AI that perceives, reasons, and acts in the real world.' Nvidia explains the evolution of AI in four major stages. First, 'Perception AI' that recognizes images and sounds; second, 'Generative AI' that creates text and images; third, 'Agentic AI' that autonomously completes tasks; and beyond that is 'Physical AI' that moves in the physical world.

The difficulty of Physical AI lies in the fact that it must 'understand' physical laws such as gravity, friction, and collisions. If a chatbot makes a mistake, it just results in confused text, but if a robot makes a mistake, it could break things or hurt people. That is why developing AI that operates safely in the real world has a completely different level of difficulty compared to generative AI.

This field suddenly became realistic at 'CES 2026,' the world's largest consumer electronics and technology trade show held in Las Vegas in January 2026. At this event, Huang declared that the 'ChatGPT moment' for Physical AI had arrived. It was a declaration that the era in which machines understand, reason, and act in the real world has come. Multiple media outlets have reported on the details of this keynote speech.
https://www.axios.com/2026/01/05/nvidia-ces-2026-jensen-huang-speech-ai

At this CES, Nvidia announced a slew of new technologies, including 'Alpamayo,' an AI for autonomous vehicles; 'GR00T,' a vision-language model for humanoid robots; 'Cosmos,' a foundation model for teaching physical laws to robots; and the next-generation semiconductor platform 'Rubin.' It was also revealed that renowned companies such as Boston Dynamics with its humanoid robot 'Atlas,' Caterpillar with its construction machinery, and Mercedes-Benz with its automobiles are adopting Nvidia's technology. Huang also indicated that robots with some human-like capabilities would appear within 2026.

sourceContent.text:
Since the arrival of ChatGPT in November 2022, our world has been filled with the term 'generative AI.' Writing text, drawing pictures, and generating code—the AI on our screens has certainly changed the way we work.

However, the person at the center of that frenzy is now beginning to talk about the 'next wave.' That person is Jensen Huang, CEO of semiconductor giant Nvidia. He has been repeatedly mentioning a figure of '$50 trillion,' a scale that is hard to believe.

In this article, I will carefully break down what the next theme Huang calls 'Physical AI' means, analyze the components of that $50 trillion figure, and explain how individual investors should approach this wave, which is being called a 'once-in-a-decade' opportunity. Along the way, I will introduce five noteworthy Japanese stocks that are not yet widely known. I have selected stocks that offer the 'joy of discovery,' rather than household names like Toyota or Sony.

Please note that this article is not intended to recommend the buying or selling of any specific stocks, but is for informational purposes only. Please make investment decisions at your own risk. The author is not an advisor with investment advisory qualifications. Now, let's begin.

To begin with, what is 'Physical AI'?—From inside the screen to the real world

Generative AI may seem omnipotent, but it actually has a major limitation: it cannot leave the screen. Even if it can create text, images, and code, it cannot pick up a cup in front of it, carry luggage, or tighten a screw.

On the other hand, the vast majority of the world's GDP is actually generated in the 'physical world.' Making, transporting, assembling, and repairing things—these labor tasks performed by humans using their bodies are the foundation of the economy. Generative AI has barely touched this massive domain.

That is why evolving AI into an 'intelligence capable of moving in the real world' is attracting attention as the next major frontier. This is the starting point of the concept of 'Physical AI.'

Defining Physical AI—'Perception,' 'Reasoning,' and 'Action'

Simply put, Physical AI is 'AI that perceives, reasons, and acts in the real world.' Nvidia explains the evolution of AI in four major stages. First, 'Perception AI' that recognizes images and sounds; second, 'Generative AI' that creates text and images; third, 'Agentic AI' that autonomously completes tasks; and beyond that is 'Physical AI' that moves in the physical world.

The difficulty of Physical AI lies in the fact that it must 'understand' physical laws such as gravity, friction, and collisions. If a chatbot makes a mistake, it just results in confused text, but if a robot makes a mistake, it could break things or hurt people. That is why developing AI that operates safely in the real world has a completely different level of difficulty compared to generative AI.

This field suddenly became realistic at 'CES 2026,' the world's largest consumer electronics and technology trade show held in Las Vegas in January 2026. At this event, Huang declared that the 'ChatGPT moment' for Physical AI had arrived. It was a declaration that the era in which machines understand, reason, and act in the real world has come. Multiple media outlets have reported on the details of this keynote speech.

https://www.axios.com/2026/01/05/nvidia-ces-2026-jensen-huang-speech-ai

At this CES, Nvidia announced a slew of new technologies, including 'Alpamayo,' an AI for autonomous vehicles; 'GR00T,' a vision-language model for humanoid robots; 'Cosmos,' a foundation model for teaching physical laws to robots; and the next-generation semiconductor platform 'Rubin.' It was also revealed that renowned companies such as Boston Dynamics with its humanoid robot 'Atlas,' Caterpillar with its construction machinery, and Mercedes-Benz with its automobiles are adopting Nvidia's technology. Huang also indicated that robots with some human-like capabilities would appear within 2026.

The following analysis article does a great job of summarizing how CES 2026 was 'all about robots and Physical AI.'

In short, the current situation is that Physical AI, which had been in the research stage, has begun to move into the 'implementation phase' as of 2026. AI that was once confined to screens is now stepping out into factories, warehouses, and roads.

The figure of $50 trillion is so massive that it feels unreal. In Japanese yen, that is well over 7,000 trillion yen. Mr. Huang is not speaking of this figure as the market size for robots alone. He is presenting it as the size of the 'entire industry that physical AI will transform'.

Specifically, this includes the massive industries of manufacturing and logistics, as well as the fields of transportation and mobility. Mr. Huang described this as 'the first $50 trillion industry that the technology sector can reach.' In other words, his argument is that the next decade will be the 'era of autonomous vehicles, robots, and autonomous machines.' You can confirm the details of this statement in the following article.

What is important is that this $50 trillion is not a 'market available right now.' It is simply the total value of the target industries that physical AI will eventually make more efficient and automate. It is accurate to understand this as the idea that if AI and robots can replace even a few percent of this massive base, a new market worth trillions of dollars will be created.

So, where is the main battlefield for this $50 trillion? We will look at it by dividing it into three major areas.

Main Battlefield 1: Automation of Factories and Logistics

The most realistic area, which is already starting to move, is the automation of factories and logistics. The introduction of robots is already underway in warehouses and production lines where labor shortages are severe. Amazon in the U.S. operates over 750,000 robots in its warehouses, automating the sorting and transport of goods. Walmart is also accelerating the automation of its logistics centers. The following article is a good reference for the expansion of this field.

https://www.nasdaq.com/articles/robotics-physical-ai-here-and-its-coming-50-trillion-market

Factories and warehouses are places where robots can perform best because the environment is organized and tasks are repetitive and predictable. Conversely, many experts believe that a future where humanoid robots walk freely around town is still far off, and for the time being, practical application will center on 'structured environments'.

The second main battlefield is autonomous driving. As Mr. Huang said at CES that 'robotaxis will be the first to benefit,' autonomous vehicles are the most easily understood example of AI moving in the real world.

At the forefront of this is Waymo, a subsidiary of Alphabet (Google's parent company). Waymo currently provides about 500,000 paid rides per week in about 10 U.S. cities, and its fleet of about 3,000 vehicles travels about 4 million miles autonomously per week. It aims to reach 1 million rides per week by the end of 2026, and its corporate value has reached approximately $126 billion.

And what Japanese individual investors cannot overlook is that Waymo plans to enter 'Tokyo,' along with London, as its first overseas expansion destination in 2026. Autonomous driving is becoming a story that is coming to our streets, not something happening far across the ocean. This plan is reported in the following article.

Meanwhile, Tesla is pursuing autonomous driving with its own 'vision-only' approach, and in China, Baidu's Apollo Go and others are commercially deployed in multiple cities. Waymo's 2026 goals and the competitive landscape are summarized in the following article.

The third, and most visionary area, is humanoids, or humanoid robots. Companies around the world, such as Tesla's 'Optimus,' Figure AI's 'Figure,' and China's Unitree and UBTECH, have entered a race for mass production of humanoid robots.

Why 'humanoid'? It is because our society is built on the premise of the 'human body.' Door heights, stair steps, tool shapes, and car driver seats are all designed to fit human dimensions. That is why the logic of those betting on humanoid robots is that if a robot has the same shape as a human, it has the potential to take over all kinds of tasks while using existing social infrastructure.

At CES, Boston Dynamics announced that it would ship its mass-produced Atlas within 2026, and it was reported that South Korea's Hyundai Motor plans to produce 30,000 units annually by 2028. The following article conveys how humanoid robots became the stars of the trade show.

How does physical AI 'move'—three computers and 'AI that learns in virtual space'

sourceContent.headline: 85% of Indian CFOs Face Pressure to Prove AI ROI: Avalara Study
sourceContent.description: Indian finance leaders are accelerating AI adoption, but governance is falling behind. Avalara finds 85% face ROI pressure, while accountability and audit readiness remain gaps.
paragraphs: An Avalara study finds Indian finance leaders are accelerating AI adoption, but governance is lagging, leaving accountability, audit readiness, and compliance gaps unresolved.

Artificial intelligence is moving from experimentation to execution inside finance departments. As AI agents become part of day-to-day financial operations, CFOs are under growing pressure to prove those investments deliver measurable business value. But as enterprises accelerate deployment, governance is struggling to keep pace.

A new global survey by Avalara suggests that Indian finance leaders are moving quickly to deploy AI agents while also facing significant governance challenges. The study points to a widening gap between AI adoption and the controls needed to manage financial risk, regulatory compliance, and accountability.

According to Avalara's report, Agents of Change: How the Race to Deploy AI Agents Is Outrunning Financial Governance, 85% of Indian finance leaders say they face moderate or significant career pressure to prove that AI agent investments are generating returns.
The survey also found that 71% believe the focus inside their organizations is on deploying AI agents quickly, while only 8% say governance takes priority over speed.
The findings suggest AI adoption is increasingly becoming a business mandate rather than just a technology initiative. However, the rush to deploy is exposing new operational risks for finance teams.
The report suggests governance frameworks have yet to catch up with the pace of AI adoption.
27% of Indian respondents said accountability for significant AI agent errors is either unclear or assigned to no one, the highest share among respondents in India, the US, the UK, and Australia.
24% have not updated internal controls in the past year to reflect AI-driven decisions.
Only 28% say AI controls have been reviewed by IT or cybersecurity teams.
10% are not confident they could clearly explain an AI agent's decisions to regulators or auditors, a higher share than respondents in the US, the UK, and Australia.
These findings suggest that while AI is increasingly influencing financial decisions, governance structures are evolving much more slowly.

Commenting on the survey findings, Dulles Krishnan, VP & General Manager, India Operations, Avalara, said: "While Indian enterprises are moving fast to automate, their internal rulebooks are being left behind. Running new AI tools on outdated compliance policies is a massive blind spot. CFOs in this market need to ensure their risk frameworks are actually updated to monitor automated decisions before an auditor comes knocking."

The findings highlight an emerging enterprise challenge. AI adoption is no longer just about automation or productivity. As AI agents begin participating in tax, compliance, and finance operations, organizations also need clear ownership, audit trails, and governance mechanisms.
Without those safeguards, faster deployment could increase regulatory and operational risk instead of reducing it.
The survey also found that 76% of Indian finance leaders lack dedicated in-house expertise to fully understand how their AI agents work.

When asked what would increase confidence in expanding AI deployment, respondents prioritized practical safeguards over additional automation. The most preferred capabilities included AI outputs grounded in verified tax and financial data (27%), human review for higher-risk actions (26%), audit trails documenting every AI action (22%), and stronger vendor commitments around accuracy and accountability (20%).
The responses suggest finance leaders are looking for explainability and oversight as much as efficiency.

sourceContent.headline: AI Infrastructure Spending Holds Near $90 Billion in Q1 2026 as ARM Overtakes x86 in Accelerated Servers; 2026 Forecast Raised to $497 Billion
sourceContent.description: IDC reports Q1 2026 AI infrastructure spending held near $90B as ARM overtook x86 in accelerated servers, with the 2026 forecast raised to $497B.
paragraphs: According to IDC's Worldwide Quarterly AI Infrastructure Tracker, spending reached $89.7 billion in Q1 2026, up 33% year-over-year but flat sequentially as growth normalizes off a larger base. The defining shift was structural: ARM-based rack-scale GPU servers overtook x86 as the dominant accelerated computing platform. IDC raised its full-year 2026 forecast to $497 billion on hyperscaler capex growth and emerging non-GPU AI demand.

The Q1 2026 results confirm that AI infrastructure investment has moved well beyond initial proof-of-concept phases into a sustained, multi-year capital commitment cycle while the competitive battle has shifted from how much compute gets bought to which platform wins it. Enterprise technology buyers, cloud service providers, and national governments are making long term decisions about where to build, how much to spend, and which AI workloads to prioritize.

For vendors, this means a prolonged period of elevated demand across accelerated compute, high-performance storage, and supporting network infrastructure, but also a fast-moving contest for architecture leadership, as ARM rackscale platforms displace x86 in the accelerated server market. For enterprises, the data signals that AI capacity is becoming a structural cost of doing business at scale, that storage refresh deferred during the initial AI buildout can no longer be postponed, and that late movers risk falling behind on both performance and cost efficiency.
IDC now projects the global AI infrastructure market will surpass $1 trillion in 2029, reaching $1.08 trillion, before climbing to $1.21 trillion in 2030.

Regional performance was mixed. The United States remained dominant at $67.9 billion (75.7% of global spend, +30.3% YoY), though growth continues to moderate. China (PRC) returned to growth at $7.8 billion (8.7% share, +9.3% YoY). The Middle East & Africa remained the fastest-growing region (+233% YoY to $1.1 billion), followed by APeJC (+62% to $5.8 billion) and Western Europe (up to $5.1 billion).

Accelerated compute remains the structural backbone, alongside a growing non-GPU AI-centric layer. Server spending represented 97.6% of total AI infrastructure value in Q1 2026, and within that, a growing share of AI-centric demand is landing on infrastructure that isn’t GPU-accelerated at all. AI orchestration tooling, data-pipeline workloads, and CPU-only inference clusters that hyperscalers are running as a cost-mitigation strategy alongside their GPU buildouts.

Deferred storage investment is catching up. After redirecting budget toward GPU and AI server spend for the past one to two years and treating storage refresh as postponable, enterprises can no longer put those purchases off. Pent-up storage refresh is now landing on top of genuine AI-driven demand, reinforcing the urgency behind external storage strategy even as AI-centric storage remains a small share (2.4%) of total AI infrastructure value.

“The Q1 2026 results make clear that AI infrastructure investment has entered a new phase where it’s not just about how much compute gets bought anymore, it’s about which platform wins it. We watched x86 accelerated servers fall from $52 billion to $35 billion in just two quarters while ARM rack-scale platforms nearly doubled, and that’s not demand destruction, that’s an architecture shift that is yet to be definitive as new x86 platforms are on the horizon as well. At the same time, we’re seeing genuine AI-driven demand show up in CPU-only inference clusters, AI orchestration tooling, and a storage refresh with a more AI-related flavor. While global economy and geopolitical tensions seem to slow down other markets, the AI investment pace continues showing an extraordinary resilience to the environment.” — Juan Seminara, Research Director, Worldwide Infrastructure Trackers, IDC
Faster-than-expected scaling of inference workloads as enterprise AI application deployment broadens
Sovereign AI program expansion in the Middle East, Southeast Asia, and Europe, driving incremental greenfield investment
New model architectures and AI agent frameworks require deeper, more distributed compute infrastructure

Emergence of non-GPU AI-centric demand (AI orchestration tooling, data-pipeline workloads, and physical AI use cases such as robotics and autonomous vehicles) extending the addressable market beyond GPU-based training and inference
Power generation and grid capacity constraints, which remain the primary operational bottleneck for new data center commissioning in major markets
Memory and storage component scarcity, which can lift server BOMs and slow procurement cycles, now compounded by enterprises simultaneously catching up on deferred storage refresh
Expanded export controls and data-sovereignty regulations, which could reshape where AI workloads are deployed and which vendors win enterprise deals

Geopolitical instability in the Middle East, where growth is concentrated in a small number of large, government-backed Gulf deals; escalation of regional tensions, including the ongoing conflict involving Iran, could delay procurement decisions, complicate data center siting and security planning, or shift government priorities away from AI infrastructure investment, introducing volatility to what is currently the fastest-growing region

Investors and technology buyers should monitor Q2 2026 capital expenditure guidance from leading hyperscalers and AI platform providers, as these forward signals remain the most reliable leading indicator of near-term infrastructure demand.
Why did AI infrastructure growth moderate from earlier 2025 peaks?

While global economy and geopolitical tensions seem to slow down other markets, the AI investment pace continues showing an extraordinary resilience to the environment.” — Juan Seminara, Research Director, Worldwide Infrastructure Trackers, IDC

Faster-than-expected scaling of inference workloads as enterprise AI application deployment broadens

Sovereign AI program expansion in the Middle East, Southeast Asia, and Europe, driving incremental greenfield investment

New model architectures and AI agent frameworks require deeper, more distributed compute infrastructure

Emergence of non-GPU AI-centric demand (AI orchestration tooling, data-pipeline workloads, and physical AI use cases such as robotics and autonomous vehicles) extending the addressable market beyond GPU-based training and inference

Power generation and grid capacity constraints, which remain the primary operational bottleneck for new data center commissioning in major markets

Memory and storage component scarcity, which can lift server BOMs and slow procurement cycles, now compounded by enterprises simultaneously catching up on deferred storage refresh

Expanded export controls and data-sovereignty regulations, which could reshape where AI workloads are deployed and which vendors win enterprise deals

Geopolitical instability in the Middle East, where growth is concentrated in a small number of large, government-backed Gulf deals; escalation of regional tensions, including the ongoing conflict involving Iran, could delay procurement decisions, complicate data center siting and security planning, or shift government priorities away from AI infrastructure investment, introducing volatility to what is currently the fastest-growing region

Investors and technology buyers should monitor Q2 2026 capital expenditure guidance from leading hyperscalers and AI platform providers, as these forward signals remain the most reliable leading indicator of near-term infrastructure demand.

Why did AI infrastructure growth moderate from earlier 2025 peaks?

Earlier quarters benefited from a step-change in capital deployment as hyperscalers accelerated training infrastructure buildouts, then a second step-change as ARM rack-scale platforms began displacing x86 in Q4 2025. Q1 2026’s 33% year-over-year growth reflects a much higher base, not a slowdown in demand. Sequential spending was essentially flat with Q4 2025’s record quarter. The long-term expansion cycle remains firmly intact, and IDC’s full-year 2026 forecast was revised upward, not downward, this quarter.

Which regions are emerging as new AI infrastructure centers?

The Middle East, particularly Saudi Arabia and the UAE, again posted the strongest year-over-year growth globally in Q1 2026, driven by government-backed sovereign AI initiatives and partnerships with leading hyperscalers, even as sequential spending pulled back from Q4 2025’s record deal flow. China returned to growth after a Q4 2025 decline. Western Europe and Asia/Pacific also grew sharply, supported by national AI strategies and localized cloud service provider expansion.

Power availability is the single most important operational constraint heading into 2026. Data center commissioning timelines are increasingly driven by utility capacity rather than hardware lead times. In parallel, evolving trade policy, particularly around advanced GPU exports, will continue to reshape competitive dynamics across China, the Middle East, and other emerging markets. The rapid ARM/x86 platform shift also raises execution risk for x86-focused OEMs and ODMs that have not yet diversified their rack-scale roadmaps.

Have ARM servers overtaken x86 in the accelerated server market, and what’s the outlook going forward?

Yes, Non-x86 (ARM) accelerated server value climbed to $53.0 billion in Q1 2026, up from $47.5 billion in Q4 2025 and $29.8 billion in Q3 2025, while x86 accelerated value fell to $34.6 billion from $42.7 billion and $51.9 billion over the same span. The crossover, which began in Q4 2025, reflects large buyers consolidating around NVL72/GB200-class rack-scale platforms and redistributing volume away from custom x86 rack designs. Projections will depend on how offerings evolve. Which platform ultimately prevails remains to be seen, as supply challenges across the industry persist.

For comprehensive vendor share, forecast data, and taxonomy detail, see: IDC Worldwide Quarterly AI Infrastructure Tracker . For taxonomy and methodology definitions, see: Worldwide Artificial Intelligence Infrastructure Tracker Taxonomy, 2025 .

Juan Pablo Seminara - Research Director, Worldwide Enterprise Infrastructure Trackers

sourceQuantifiedLines.line: AI Infrastructure Spending Holds Near $90 Billion in Q1 2026 as ARM Overtakes x86 in Accelerated Servers; 2026 Forecast Raised to $497 Billion
According to IDC's Worldwide Quarterly AI Infrastructure Tracker, spending reached $89.7 billion in Q1 2026, up 33% year-over-year but flat sequentially as growth normalizes off a larger base.
IDC raised its full-year 2026 forecast to $497 billion on hyperscaler capex growth and emerging non-GPU AI demand.
IDC now projects the global AI infrastructure market will surpass $1 trillion in 2029, reaching $1.08 trillion, before climbing to $1.21 trillion in 2030.
The United States remained dominant at $67.9 billion (75.7% of global spend, +30.3% YoY), though growth continues to moderate.
China (PRC) returned to growth at $7.8 billion (8.7% share, +9.3% YoY).
The Middle East & Africa remained the fastest-growing region (+233% YoY to $1.1 billion), followed by APeJC (+62% to $5.8 billion) and Western Europe (up to $5.1 billion).
Server spending represented 97.6% of total AI infrastructure value in Q1 2026, and within that, a growing share of AI-centric demand is landing on infrastructure that isn’t GPU-accelerated at all.

Pent-up storage refresh is now landing on top of genuine AI-driven demand, reinforcing the urgency behind external storage strategy even as AI-centric storage remains a small share (2.4%) of total AI infrastructure value.

We watched x86 accelerated servers fall from $52 billion to $35 billion in just two quarters while ARM rack-scale platforms nearly doubled, and that’s not demand destruction, that’s an architecture shift that is yet to be definitive as new x86 platforms are on the horizon as well.
Q1 2026’s 33% year-over-year growth reflects a much higher base, not a slowdown in demand.

Yes, Non-x86 (ARM) accelerated server value climbed to $53.0 billion in Q1 2026, up from $47.5 billion in Q4 2025 and $29.8 billion in Q3 2025, while x86 accelerated value fell to $34.6 billion from $42.7 billion and $51.9 billion over the same span.

sourceContent.description: Global spending on AI infrastructure reached $89.7 billion in Q1 2026, representing a 33.1 percent increase year on year, according to IDC
paragraphs: Global spending on AI infrastructure reached $89.7 billion in the first quarter of 2026, representing a 33.1 percent increase year on year, according to IDC’s Worldwide Quarterly AI Infrastructure Tracker.

While spending on AI infrastructure remained flat compared with the previous quarter as growth normalized from a higher base, AI infrastructure market has entered a new phase driven by long-term investment commitments, architecture shifts, and expanding enterprise AI deployments.

IDC has raised its full-year 2026 AI infrastructure spending forecast to $497 billion, reflecting continued hyperscaler capital expenditure, growing enterprise adoption, and rising demand for AI infrastructure beyond GPU-based computing. The global AI infrastructure market will exceed $1.08 trillion in 2029 before reaching $1.21 trillion in 2030, representing a five-year CAGR of approximately 30 percent from 2025.

A major trend in Q1 2026 was the transition from traditional x86 accelerated servers to ARM-based rack-scale GPU platforms, which have become the leading architecture for AI workloads. IDC reported that non-x86 (ARM) accelerated servers generated $53.0 billion in spending during the quarter, compared with $34.6 billion for x86 systems, highlighting a significant shift in AI data center deployments, Juan Seminara, Research Director, Worldwide Infrastructure Trackers, IDC, said in a blog post .

Server infrastructure dominated AI spending, accounting for $87.6 billion, or 97.6 percent of total AI infrastructure investment. Storage spending reached $2.2 billion, representing 2.4 percent of the market. There is growing demand for AI orchestration software, CPU-only inference clusters, and data pipeline infrastructure as hyperscalers seek lower-cost alternatives for selected AI workloads.
United States Maintains Leadership While Middle East Records Fastest Growth

The United States remained the world’s largest AI infrastructure market with $67.9 billion in spending during Q1 2026, representing 75.7 percent of global investment and growing 30.3 percent year over year.
China returned to growth with $7.8 billion, accounting for 8.7 percent of worldwide spending and expanding 9.3 percent compared with a year earlier.

The Middle East and Africa emerged as the fastest-growing region globally, with spending increasing 233 percent year over year to $1.1 billion, supported by sovereign AI initiatives and government-backed investments.

Asia Pacific excluding Japan and China (APeJC) region recorded 62 percent growth to $5.8 billion, while Western Europe reached $5.1 billion as governments and enterprises accelerated AI infrastructure deployment.
AI Infrastructure Spending Continues Multi-Year Expansion
Global AI infrastructure spending reached $318 billion in 2025, more than doubling from $153 billion in 2024, which itself represented 107.6 percent year-over-year growth.

AI infrastructure investment has evolved beyond experimental deployments into a structural, long-term capital investment cycle. Enterprises are also beginning to refresh storage infrastructure after delaying upgrades during the initial wave of GPU investments, creating additional demand across storage systems alongside AI servers.
AI infrastructure spending will expand by approximately 56 percent in 2026, an upward revision from its previous estimate of around 53 percent growth.

Key factors supporting expansion include deployment of enterprise AI inference workloads, increasing sovereign AI programs across the Middle East, Southeast Asia, and Europe, adoption of AI agents and next-generation AI models requiring distributed computing, and growing investment in non-GPU AI infrastructure supporting orchestration platforms, robotics, autonomous vehicles, and AI data pipelines.

However, there are risks that could affect future growth. These include electricity generation and grid capacity limitations delaying new data center construction, shortages of memory and storage components, tighter export controls on advanced AI hardware, evolving data sovereignty regulations, and geopolitical uncertainty affecting AI investments in rapidly growing regions such as the Middle East.

sourceContent.description: Worldwide end-user spending on AI models and platforms is projected to total US$64 billion in 2026, up 63.4 per cent from US$39 billion in 2025, with more and more enterprises are choosing to work with companies that can provide clear value. Spending on generative AI (genAI) models is forecast to grow 117 per cent while AI platform spending will rise […]
paragraphs: Providers who embed oversight and AI management will have an edge.

Worldwide end-user spending on AI models and platforms is projected to total US$64 billion in 2026, up 63.4 per cent from US$39 billion in 2025, with more and more enterprises are choosing to work with companies that can provide clear value.

Spending on generative AI (genAI) models is forecast to grow 117 per cent while AI platform spending will rise 36.9 per cent in 2026, according to Gartner’s latest forecast on AI platforms and models.

“Enterprise AI budgets are coming under greater scrutiny, with increased focus on usage efficiency, cost control and measurable outcomes ,” said the analyst firm’s senior principal research analyst, Arunasree Cheparthi.
“Spending is shifting toward providers who can demonstrate clear value across cost, latency, performance, and reliability.
“This is giving an edge to providers that embed evaluation, cost transparency, and usage tracking into customer workflows, making it easier to manage and optimise AI use.”
However, as spending becomes more usage-driven, providers face pressure to demonstrate real adoption, sustained use, and durable margins.
This dynamic is accelerating growth in domain-specific language models (DSLMs) and specialised models, which are forecast to grow 210 percent in 2026.

According to Gartner, the AI software market is forecast to grow significantly between 2025 and 2026, with total market revenue increasing from US$39.3 billion to US$64.3 billion, representing 63.4 per cent growth.
The Foundation Generative AI Models segment is expected to more than double, rising from US$11.4 billion in 2025 to US$23.4 billion in 2026, representing a growth rate of 104.2 per cent.
Meanwhile, the fastest-growing segment is DSLMs and specialised genAI models, which is projected to expand from US$1.6 billion to US$4.9 billion, achieving 210.0 per cent growth.

AI application development platforms are forecast to grow from US$6.9 billion to US$9.5 billion (up 38.6 per cent), and AI platforms for data science and machine learning are expected to increase from US$19.4 billion to US$26.4 billion (an increase of 36.3 per cent).
Overall, these projections highlight accelerating investment in generative AI technologies, particularly in specialised AI and foundation models .
“Over the long-term, the biggest winners will be vendors that help enterprises manage where and how AI is used across the business ,” said Cheparthi.

“As more models enter the market and usage-based pricing becomes harder to predict, buyers will turn to platforms that help them choose the right tools, monitor performance , enforce policy and keep costs under control.”

sourceContent.text:
Providers who embed oversight and AI management will have an edge.

Worldwide end-user spending on AI models and platforms is projected to total US$64 billion in 2026, up 63.4 per cent from US$39 billion in 2025, with more and more enterprises are choosing to work with companies that can provide clear value.

Spending on generative AI (genAI) models is forecast to grow 117 per cent while AI platform spending will rise 36.9 per cent in 2026, according to Gartner’s latest forecast on AI platforms and models.

“Enterprise AI budgets are coming under greater scrutiny, with increased focus on usage efficiency, cost control and measurable outcomes ,” said the analyst firm’s senior principal research analyst, Arunasree Cheparthi.

“Spending is shifting toward providers who can demonstrate clear value across cost, latency, performance, and reliability.

“This is giving an edge to providers that embed evaluation, cost transparency, and usage tracking into customer workflows, making it easier to manage and optimise AI use.”

However, as spending becomes more usage-driven, providers face pressure to demonstrate real adoption, sustained use, and durable margins.

This dynamic is accelerating growth in domain-specific language models (DSLMs) and specialised models, which are forecast to grow 210 percent in 2026.

According to Gartner, the AI software market is forecast to grow significantly between 2025 and 2026, with total market revenue increasing from US$39.3 billion to US$64.3 billion, representing 63.4 per cent growth.

The Foundation Generative AI Models segment is expected to more than double, rising from US$11.4 billion in 2025 to US$23.4 billion in 2026, representing a growth rate of 104.2 per cent.

Meanwhile, the fastest-growing segment is DSLMs and specialised genAI models, which is projected to expand from US$1.6 billion to US$4.9 billion, achieving 210.0 per cent growth.

AI application development platforms are forecast to grow from US$6.9 billion to US$9.5 billion (up 38.6 per cent), and AI platforms for data science and machine learning are expected to increase from US$19.4 billion to US$26.4 billion (an increase of 36.3 per cent).

Overall, these projections highlight accelerating investment in generative AI technologies, particularly in specialised AI and foundation models .

“Over the long-term, the biggest winners will be vendors that help enterprises manage where and how AI is used across the business ,” said Cheparthi.

“As more models enter the market and usage-based pricing becomes harder to predict, buyers will turn to platforms that help them choose the right tools, monitor performance , enforce policy and keep costs under control.”

${title} ${date} ${LTP} Vol.${VOLUME} ${CHANGE} ${change_PERC}%
Spending on generative AI models is expected to grow 117% in 2026, while AI platforms are forecasted to increase by 36.9%

Worldwide end-user spending on artificial intelligence (AI) platforms and models is projected to reach $64 billion in 2026, up 63.4 per cent from $39 billion in 2025, according to a report by Gartner, a business and technology insights company.
It highlighted that spending on generative AI (GenAI) models is expected to grow 117 per cent in 2026, while spending on AI platforms is forecast to increase 36.9 per cent during the year.

According to Gartner, enterprise AI spending is entering a new phase, with companies paying greater attention to how efficiently AI is being used, how much it costs and whether it delivers measurable business outcomes.

"Enterprise AI budgets are coming under greater scrutiny, with increased focus on usage efficiency, cost control and measurable outcomes," said Arunasree Cheparthi, Senior Principal Research Analyst at Gartner. She said spending is increasingly shifting towards AI providers that can demonstrate value across cost, latency, performance and reliability.

"This is giving an edge to providers that embed evaluation, cost transparency and usage tracking into customer workflows, making it easier to manage and optimise AI use. However, as spending becomes more usage-driven, providers face increasing pressure to demonstrate real adoption, sustained use and durable margins," Cheparthi added.

The report said this trend is driving rapid growth in domain-specific language models (DSLMs) and specialised AI models, which are expected to record the fastest growth among all segments. According to the forecast, spending on Foundation Generative AI Models will increase from $11.4 billion in 2025 to $23.4 billion in 2026, registering a growth of 104.2 per cent.
Meanwhile, spending on DSLMs and Specialised GenAI Models is expected to rise from $1.6 billion to $4.9 billion, marking a 210 per cent increase in 2026.

The report also projected spending on AI Application Development Platforms to increase from $6.9 billion in 2025 to $9.5 billion in 2026, while spending on AI Platforms for Data Science and Machine Learning is expected to rise from $19.4 billion to $26.4 billion during the same period.
Looking ahead, Gartner said vendors that help enterprises manage AI usage across their businesses are likely to benefit the most as the market evolves.

sourceContent.headline: Global AI platforms and models market to grow 63 pc to USD 64 billion in 2026: Gartner
sourceContent.description: Worldwide end-user spending on artificial intelligence (AI) platforms and models is projected to reach USD 64 billion in 2026, up 63.4 per cent from USD 39 billion in 2025, according to a report by Gartner, a business and technology insights company.
paragraphs: New Delhi [India], July 20 (ANI): Worldwide end-user spending on artificial intelligence (AI) platforms and models is projected to reach USD 64 billion in 2026, up 63.4 per cent from USD 39 billion in 2025, according to a report by Gartner, a business and technology insights company. It highlighted that spending on generative AI (GenAI) models is expected to grow 117 per cent in 2026, while spending on AI platforms is forecast to increase 36.9 per cent during the year. According to Gartner, enterprise AI spending is entering a new phase, with companies paying greater attention to how efficiently AI is being used, how much it costs and whether it delivers measurable business outcomes. "Enterprise AI budgets are coming under greater scrutiny, with increased focus on usage efficiency, cost control and measurable outcomes," said Arunasree Cheparthi, Senior Principal Research Analyst at Gartner. She said spending is increasingly shifting towards AI providers that can demonstrate value across cost, latency, performance and reliability.

"This is giving an edge to providers that embed evaluation, cost transparency and usage tracking into customer workflows, making it easier to manage and optimise AI use. However, as spending becomes more usage-driven, providers face increasing pressure to demonstrate real adoption, sustained use and durable margins," Cheparthi added. The report said this trend is driving rapid growth in domain-specific language models (DSLMs) and specialised AI models, which are expected to record the fastest growth among all segments. According to the forecast, spending on Foundation Generative AI Models will increase from USD 11.4 billion in 2025 to USD 23.4 billion in 2026, registering a growth of 104.2 per cent. Meanwhile, spending on DSLMs and Specialised GenAI Models is expected to rise from USD 1.6 billion to USD 4.9 billion, marking a 210 per cent increase in 2026. The report also projected spending on AI Application Development Platforms to increase from USD 6.9 billion in 2025 to USD 9.5 billion in 2026, while spending on AI Platforms for Data Science and Machine Learning is expected to rise from USD 19.4 billion to USD 26.4 billion during the same period. Looking ahead, Gartner said vendors that help enterprises manage AI usage across their businesses are likely to benefit the most as the market evolves. (ANI)

paragraphs: High margin AI product growth plan builds on Company’s reported 147% YOY revenue growth and $6.6 million net profit from operations in H1 2026.
Genius OS integrates AI Agent teams across Genius School, Genius Academy, Genius Resorts and Genius City models.
Genius OS links to over 300 leading AI models including the latest models from Hermes, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, SpaceX, Meta, Deepseek and Alibaba.
AI product integration follows success of Student AI and Teacher AI, which have scaled to 300,000 users globally in 2026.

SINGAPORE, July 21, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Genius Group Limited (NYSE American: GNS) ( "Genius Group" , "GNS" or the "Company" ), a leading AI-powered education group, today announced the launch of its full AI-powered product suite, Genius OS. Genius OS is a cohesive family of AI-agent-driven solutions delivering education, acceleration and productivity to students, entrepreneurs and investors across the Company’s four revenue drivers: Genius School, Genius Academy, Genius Resorts and Genius City. Genius Group is rolling out early access to Genius OS initially to its six million students globally, with new users invited to apply for access at www.geniusgroup.ai .

Roger Hamilton, CEO of Genius Group said “We believe the current AI wave is the unique opportunity for a revolution in education to personalized, gamified learning. According to Research and Markets, the AI in education market is forecast to grow 300% from approximately US$10.6 billion in 2026 to US$42.48 billion by 2030 [1] . At this unique moment when AI is moving from single tools to AI agents that act on your behalf, Genius Group has built a full suite of AI agents for every student, entrepreneur and investor we serve .”
The suite spans the Company’s four revenue drivers and is delivered through one operating system and one AI agent layer. Its core products are as follows:

Genius School: A Genius OS suite for teachers and students at primary and secondary school, based on the success of Student AI (studentai.app) and Teacher AI (teacherai.app), with personalized courses for international systems across K-12, Cambridge and International Baccalaureate (IB) curricula.

AI Academy: A Genius OS suite for companies seeking AI talent and AI talent building certified AI skills. Our AI Academy is positioned to be a world leading AI Talent & Training platform, launching with over 100 AI certification microcourses from the world’s leading AI providers, and personalized matches to over 100,000 open AI jobs and over 1,000,000 AI experts.

Entrepreneur Academy: A Genius OS suite for entrepreneurs to build AI agent teams to support their startups and scale up enterprises, with AI agent specialists in planning, market research, product design, coding, marketing, sales and delivery. AI agent specialists in legals, finance, operations and HR enable business owners to redesign their companies into AI-first enterprises.

Investor Academy: A Genius OS suite for investors to build AI agent teams to support their investment portfolio, extending AI powered portfolio management tools for its Company’s Property Investor Network to AI agent teams across property, equities, commodities and digital assets with specialists in market trends, deal sourcing, matchmaking, risk analysis, portfolio optimization, funding access, investor marketplace and legals internationally.

Genius Resorts: A mobile app, Genie AI, which powers learning communities to earn and learn with GEMs, attracting a network of partners to provide impact-focused learning journeys and apprenticeships, with GEMs earned and redeemed with local vendors including event venues, restaurants, stores and learning centers. The GPS-enabled, Genie AI pilot is launching in Bali, Indonesia, the home of the first Genius City, at the end of July 2026.

Genius City: An internal Genius OS suite which Genius is utilizing to self-improve its AI powered offerings, with a focus on community-driven, values-centered sovereign AI in which each Genius City owns its own AI powered economy with blockchain-based transparency on the ownership of the enterprises within each Genius City. The Company intends to apply the AI powered transparency and analytics tools it is creating towards the trading of its publicly owned shares with the aim of improving transparency and fair markets for the benefit of all stakeholders.

Genius Group’s AI product strategy capitalizes on two of the fastest-growing markets in technology, alongside a rapidly expanding base of AI users. According to Research and Markets, the AI in education market is forecast to grow from approximately US$10.6 billion in 2026 to US$42.48 billion by 2030 [1] . According to Markets and Markets, the AI agents market is forecast to grow from US$7.84 billion in 2025 to US$52.62 billion by 2030 [2] . And according to Statista, the number of AI tool users worldwide has grown from around 255 million in 2023 toward a projected 700 million by 2030 [3] . Genius Group combines the distribution of a 6 million user base with a proprietary AI operating system and agent layer, positioning it to convert our audience into recurring, high-margin AI product revenue.

The demand for AI skills is accelerating in step. According to the World Economic Forum, 77% of employers plan to upskill their workforce by 2030, with AI and big data among the fastest-growing skill sets [4] . According to PwC’s Global AI Jobs Barometer, workers with AI skills already command a wage premium of 56% [5] . The cost of the gap is steep: according to IDC, technology skills shortages could cost organizations up to US$5.5 trillion by 2026 [6] .

The Company believes that the launch of its integrated AI product suite is a timely step towards meeting this high demand for AI upskilling of students, teachers, entrepreneurs, investors and enterprises globally.

[1] Research and Markets, Artificial Intelligence in Education Market. AI in education forecast to grow from US$10.6 billion in 2026 to US$42.48 billion by 2030. https://www.researchandmarkets.com/report/education-ai

[2] Markets and Markets, AI Agents Market. AI agents forecast to grow from US$7.84 billion in 2025 to US$52.62 billion by 2030 (46.3% CAGR). https://www.marketsandmarkets.com/PressReleases/ai-agents.asp

sourceContent.description: The global dental services market is projected to grow from USD 523.98 billion in 2026 to USD 795.72 billion by 2035, driven by rising demand for cosmetic and restorative procedures, increasing oral health awareness, and the adoption of digital dentistry technologies.
paragraphs: The global Dental Services Market was valued at USD 499.32 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach USD 795.72 billion by 2035, expanding at a CAGR of 4.77% from 2026 to 2035. Market growth is driven by the rising prevalence of oral diseases, increasing demand for cosmetic and restorative dental procedures, and rapid adoption of digital dentistry technologies such as AI-powered diagnostics, CAD/CAM systems, 3D imaging, and teledentistry. Growing oral health awareness, expanding dental tourism, and investments in advanced dental infrastructure are further supporting global market expansion.
What Is Driving the Growth of the Dental Services Market?

The global dental services market is expanding steadily, driven by rising oral disease prevalence, increasing demand for cosmetic dental procedures, and the adoption of digital dentistry technologies . The market size was valued at USD 499.32 billion in 2025 and is projected to grow from USD 523.98 billion in 2026 to USD 795.72 billion by 2035, registering a CAGR of 4.77% from 2026 to 2035.
North America dominated the market with a major market share of 46% in 2025.
Asia Pacific is expected to grow at the fastest CAGR between 2026 and 2035.
By procedure, the non-cosmetic dentistry segment contributed the highest market share in 2025.
By procedure, the cosmetic dentistry segment is growing at a strong CAGR between 2026 and 2035.
By service, the oral surgery segment held a major market share in 2025.
By service, the orthodontics & prosthodontics segment is expected to expand at a notable CAGR from 2026 to 2035.
By end user, the dental clinics segment generated the biggest market share in 2025.
By end user, the hospitals segment is expanding at the fastest CAGR between 2026 and 2035.

The dental services market involves the diagnosis, prevention, and treatment of oral diseases, tooth loss, and structural defects. This market generates revenue from clinics and practitioners and is categorized into three main areas, including preventive care for maintaining oral hygiene, restorative treatments like root canals and dentures for repairing damage, and cosmetic procedures such as implants and teeth whitening to enhance appearance. The growth of this market is driven by the increasing prevalence of oral diseases, advancements in technology, and a heightened consumer focus on aesthetic procedures, which fuel the demand for routine care and improved treatment precision.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is revolutionizing the global market by improving precision in X-ray and 3D image analysis, assisting in treatment planning, and automating administrative tasks. AI algorithms are shifting dentistry from reactive, human-reliant assessments to highly precise, data-driven workflows. For instance, AI can instantly analyze dental radiographs and intraoral scans to detect early signs of cavities, gum disease, and anatomical irregularities, often identifying issues that a human eye might overlook. AI is widely used in orthodontics and implantology to model precise changes before operations commence.

Transformation of Workflows with AI and CAD/CAM : AI-assisted diagnostics help detect early signs of decay and gum disease, allowing for precise orthodontic treatment planning. Technologies like 3D printing and CAD/CAM enable same-day crowns, veneers, and aligners, leading to increased investment in digital workflows that enhance treatment accuracy and patient convenience.

Growing Demand for Cosmetic and Restorative Dentistry : With an increased focus on aesthetics driven by social media and an aging population, cosmetic procedures are in high demand . Invisible orthodontics are becoming popular among adults and teens, replacing traditional metal braces. Lasers are also being used more frequently for pain-free gum sculpting, cavity removal, and accelerated teeth whitening.

Consolidation and the Rise of Dental Service Organizations (DSOs) : The market is experiencing a shift towards corporate consolidation and the establishment of organized dental chains. DSOs handle the business and administrative aspects of dental clinics, allowing dentists to focus on clinical care while scaling operations, standardizing treatment, and expanding access to specialized procedures.

The Shift toward Proactive Oral Health : As awareness of oral hygiene increases, the focus is shifting toward convenience and early, remote intervention. Teledentistry platforms are being utilized for video consultations , reducing the need for in-office visits and allowing for preventative care rather than only reacting to emergencies.

The growing prevalence of dental caries and other oral diseases among the global population is driving the demand for the dental services across the globe. According to the data published by the FDI World Dental Federation, in 2015, around 3.5 billion people were suffering from some kind of oral diseases across the globe. The most common oral health condition was the untreated decay of permanent teeth. The various other factors that drive the market include the rising popularity of dental tourism , increasing demand for the cosmetic dentistry , growing dental implants , and technological advancements in dental services.

The growing awareness regarding oral health among the population, rising disposable income, and rising investments in developing healthcare infrastructure are the key factors responsible for the growth of the dental services market globally. The surging importance of dental support organizations is playing an important role in altering the delivery model of the dental services. The growth of various dental support organizations has significantly fostered the in-house dental services. Dental support organizations are centers that make contracts with the dental service providers and offers management services to provide non-clinical dental services to the consumers. According to the American Dental Association, around 16.3% of the dentists of US were partnered with dental support organizations in 2017. The introduction of invisible teeth braces or aligners have gained rapid traction among the consumers. Moreover, the growing concerns among the young population regarding their aesthetic appearances have encouraged the growth of the global dental services market.

Industry growth Overview: The demand for the dental services industry is being driven by developing digital dentistry solutions such as CAD/CAM systems,3D imaging, lasers, and clear aligners, which creates possibilities for worldwide dental tech companies to reveal localized and advanced solutions.

Global Expansion: Across various cultures, regular practices have continued to encourage oral hygiene routines. In several Middle Eastern and African countries, Miswak sticks have been made from the Salvadora persica tree, which is widely used for its natural antibacterial elements. Such twigs have been utilized for centuries as environment-friendly choices to current toothbrushes, which market oral cleanliness with less environmental impact.

Sustainability Trends: Sustainable practices place importance on utilizing non-toxic and secure materials for fillings, prosthetics, and several other dental implements. This lowers the risk of different feedback and markets complete patient health. Dental practices that concentrate on sustainability are more likely to use environmentally friendly sterilization and cleaning procedures and are less likely to release toxic volatile compounds.

Startup Ecosystem: The startup companies are concentrating on virtual care platforms and tele dentistry. Such digital solutions allow patients to consult with dentists remotely, which enables educational links, and even receive a particular diagnosis from the convenience of their homes. Tele dentistry not only develops access to care, specifically in undeveloped spaces, but also promotes higher flexibility and ease for practitioners and patients alike. Additionally, there is a rising importance on eco-friendliness and sustainability within the dental industry.

The dental services market is primarily driven by the increasing prevalence of oral diseases such as dental caries, periodontal conditions, and tooth loss, which are rising due to changing dietary habits and poor oral hygiene. Growing awareness of oral health and its connection to overall health is also encouraging more people to seek preventive and routine dental care. Additionally, expanding access to dental insurance and improvements in dental technologies such as digital imaging, laser dentistry, and minimally invasive procedures are further supporting market growth.

According to the World Health Organization (WHO), oral diseases pose a major health burden for many countries, affecting people throughout their lifetime and even causing death. It is estimated that oral diseases affect nearly 3.7 billion people.

The Rapid Shift Toward AI-Powered and Digitized Workflows

Digital dentistry and AI are transforming clinical practices by optimizing diagnostics and treatment planning. Technologies such as AI-enabled caries detection, 3D printing, and teledentistry are streamlining workflows, improving accuracy, and reducing appointment times. This technological shift enhances the patient experience, alleviates dental anxiety, and provides holistic, evidence-based care while facilitating high-efficiency operations.

For instance, Overjet is an FDA-cleared dental AI platform adopted by major DSOs to standardize clinical care, increase treatment acceptance, and automate insurance documentation, thus improving diagnostic accuracy and operational efficiency. (Source: https://www.who.int )

Despite its revolutionary potential, the dental services market often faces obstacles due to the high out-of-pocket costs associated with advanced procedures, limiting accessibility. The industry struggles with health insurance reimbursement structures, where global trends heavily rely on out-of-pocket payments for cosmetic and restorative care. Furthermore, workforce shortages and disparities in care access hinder broader commercialization and market penetration.
