ChatGPT just lost a title it held since the day it launched. Sensor Tower’s State of AI 2026 report puts OpenAI’s chatbot at 46.4% of the global AI-assistant market at the end of May 2026, the first time it has held less than half the market since debuting in November 2022. Google’s Gemini climbed to 27.7% over the same period, and Anthropic’s Claude reached 10.3%, according to the same tracking data reported by TechCrunch on June 16, 2026 .

ChatGPT’s Market Share Falls Below 50% for the First Time

The Numbers Behind the Slide: Three Trackers, One Story

Claude’s Enterprise Play: How Anthropic Is Cutting Into OpenAI’s Lead

Australia’s AI Adoption Numbers: Telsyte’s June 2026 Snapshot

Market Share vs Revenue: Why OpenAI Still Leads on Money

Competitive Comparison: ChatGPT vs Gemini vs Claude at a Glance

Historical Context: How Fast Tech Leaders Usually Lose Ground

What This Means for Australian Businesses Choosing an AI Vendor

Market Impact: Why Investors and Analysts Are Watching Closely

Five Predictions: Where AI Assistant Market Share Goes Next

Does ChatGPT’s falling market share mean it’s losing users?

The shift shows up just as clearly in Australia. Telsyte’s June 2026 research counts more than 17 million Australians using AI tools monthly, but ChatGPT’s local lead is narrowing too: 13.8 million users against Gemini’s 9.1 million and Claude’s 2.9 million, per Telsyte’s announcement . Nearly four in five Australian AI adopters still use ChatGPT specifically, but that ratio is under real pressure for the first time since the category existed.

Add Tech Insider once in the Google app and our stories appear in your news suggestions.

Sensor Tower measures what it calls “True Audience,” the number of unique people using a product across both mobile apps and the web in a given month. By that measure, ChatGPT’s global AI-assistant market share slipped under the 50% mark in March 2026 and kept falling, landing at 46.4% by the end of May. A year earlier, in December 2024, ChatGPT held 65.3% of the same market. Eighteen months of steady erosion turned a near-monopoly into a plurality.

OpenAI is not shrinking. It is growing more slowly than its rivals. ChatGPT still adds tens of millions of users every quarter, but Gemini and Claude are adding them faster, and that gap is what shows up in the share numbers. It is the classic pattern of a market maturing: the pioneer keeps growing in absolute terms while newer entrants eat into its share of the total pie.

Sensor Tower is not the only firm seeing this. Analytics provider Apptopia, first reported by Big Technology and later covered by Fortune , tracked ChatGPT’s app market share falling from 69.1% in January 2025 to 45.3% earlier in 2026, while Gemini’s app share rose from 14.7% to 25.2% across the same window. Similarweb’s web-traffic numbers, published June 11 using data through May 26, put ChatGPT’s global web traffic share at 52.7%, down from 56.7% in March and roughly 87% in early 2025.

The table below lines up the key data points from Sensor Tower’s tracking of the global AI-assistant market, cross-checked against Similarweb’s independent web-traffic figures.

Source: Sensor Tower’s State of AI 2026 report and Similarweb data, as compiled by TechCrunch and TechnologyChecker .

Read across the rows and the pattern is hard to miss. ChatGPT’s line points down in every period. Gemini’s and Claude’s point up in every period. None of the individual moves looks dramatic month to month, but stacked across eighteen months they add up to the biggest reshuffling the AI-assistant market has seen since ChatGPT created the category in the first place.

Gemini’s growth story is mostly a distribution story. Google folded Gemini into Search, Android, and Workspace rather than asking users to go find and install a separate app, and that bundling shows up directly in the numbers: Gemini’s monthly active users reached 662 million by May 2026, up from a 6% market share in early 2025 to 27.7% by May. Paid conversion sits at a modest 3.1%, far behind Claude’s rate, which tells you Gemini’s growth is coming from reach rather than from users paying for premium tiers.

There is a wrinkle worth flagging. Gemini’s share of new app downloads actually cooled in the second quarter of 2026, dropping to 22% from a peak of 34% in the final quarter of 2025. Usage share and download share are not the same metric, and the gap between them suggests Gemini’s edge now comes more from being pre-installed and cross-promoted across Google’s ecosystem than from people actively choosing to seek it out and download it fresh.

Claude’s consumer numbers look small next to ChatGPT and Gemini: 245 million monthly active users and 10.3% of the assistant market in May 2026. But two other figures explain why Anthropic gets outsized attention from investors and enterprise buyers. Claude converts free users to paid subscribers at 13.0%, the highest rate among the major assistants tracked. And on the enterprise side, where companies pay for API access rather than consumer subscriptions, Anthropic has pulled ahead of OpenAI entirely.

Menlo Ventures, an Anthropic investor that runs an annual survey of enterprise AI spending, put Anthropic’s share of enterprise large language model spend at roughly a third of the market in 2026, ahead of OpenAI’s mid-20s percentage and Google’s share in the low 20s. Anthropic built that lead on coding tools and agentic workflows, categories where Claude models have consistently ranked well on independent benchmarks. Consumer market share grabs headlines. Enterprise spend share is what pays the bills.

Telsyte’s June 2026 research is the clearest local read on how the global shift is playing out for Australian users specifically. The research firm counts Australia’s total AI user base at more than 17 million people, with 80% of them engaging monthly rather than trying a tool once and dropping it.

Nearly four in five Australian AI adopters still use ChatGPT specifically, according to Telsyte, so it remains the default choice by a wide margin locally. But the runner-up field is getting crowded. Gemini’s local user base is already two-thirds the size of ChatGPT’s, and separate research from ROI.com.au found 58% of Australians now use AI tools monthly overall, that two in three Australian workers use AI on the job, and that more than half of them do it without their employer’s sign-off. Roughly 43% of Australian small and medium businesses report using AI in some form, a figure that keeps climbing as procurement teams catch up to what staff are already doing informally.

Losing market share is not the same as losing the business. OpenAI’s weekly active users crossed 900 million on February 27, 2026, and monthly active users passed 1 billion in June 2026, making ChatGPT the fastest app in history to reach that milestone, according to Sensor Tower data reported by TechCrunch. Annualized revenue crossed $25 billion by February 2026, up from roughly $20 billion in 2025 and $6 billion in 2024. Mobile app revenue alone hit $1.35 billion in 2025, up 673% year over year from $174 million in 2024.

Put the two data sets side by side and a fuller picture appears. ChatGPT’s share of the market is shrinking while its user base and revenue keep climbing, because the overall AI-assistant market is expanding faster than ChatGPT alone can capture. Roughly $25 billion in annualized revenue against 1.1 billion monthly users works out to an implied $20-something per user per year, though the real split is far more concentrated: a smaller base of paying subscribers and enterprise API customers accounts for most of that revenue, not the free-tier majority. OpenAI is still winning in absolute terms. It is just no longer winning by default.

Consumer app downloads and enterprise API contracts are two different markets that get lumped together in casual conversation. The enterprise numbers matter more for long-term revenue, because API contracts tend to be larger, stickier, and less price-sensitive than consumer subscriptions.

Figures are from Menlo Ventures’ 2026 enterprise AI survey, as reported by Fortune. The remainder of enterprise spend splits across smaller providers including Meta’s open Llama models, Mistral, and various in-house deployments. Anthropic’s enterprise lead is arguably the single most important number in this story for anyone managing an AI budget rather than chatting after hours, because it suggests the consumer market-share headline and the enterprise buying decision are pointing in different directions entirely.

Line the three leaders up and each one is winning a different contest. ChatGPT still has the largest audience and the most revenue by a wide margin, and it remains the default answer to “which AI should I use” for most consumers. Gemini wins on distribution, riding Android and Search into hundreds of millions of users who never had to make an active choice to adopt it. Claude wins on monetization efficiency and enterprise trust, converting a smaller user base into disproportionate revenue and API spend.

None of the three is winning outright, which is itself the headline. Eighteen months ago, this would have been a one-horse race. Now it is a genuine three-way contest with different providers leading on different metrics. For a broader look at how these and other systems stack up on benchmarks and pricing, see our guide to the best AI models of 2026 .

sourceContent.headline: OpenAI Financials Leaked Ahead Of IPO? ChatGPT Maker Said To Have Lost $39B Last Year: Here's How That Compares To Anthropic, SpaceX
sourceContent.description: The figures are likely to face close scrutiny from investors, especially if OpenAI and Anthropic launch IPOs around the same time.
paragraphs: OpenAI spent $34 billion on various expenses last year, according to a Financial Times report.

OpenAI’s net loss widened from $5 billion in 2024 to about $39 billion in 2025, the Financial Times reported. Excluding restructuring charges and other non-cash items, the company’s loss was $8 billion.
The AI company confidentially filed for a U.S. IPO last week.

OpenAI’s net loss ballooned from $5 billion in 2024 to a staggering $39 billion last year, as it continued to spend heavily on AI model development and securing compute capacity, the Financial Times reported on Tuesday, citing audited financial figures confirmed by its sources.
The ChatGPT maker spent $34 billion last year, including $19 billion on research and development and nearly $6 billion on sales, marketing, and other expenses, according to the report .

Coming just after OpenAI confidentially filed for a U.S. IPO, the reported figures highlight the sheer scale of spending at the AI giant as it faces intensifying competition from Anthropic and Google. The numbers are likely to come under close scrutiny from prospective investors, especially as OpenAI and Anthropic could launch their IPOs around the same time.
On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment was ‘neutral’ for OPEAZZX and ‘bullish’ for ANTHZZX early Tuesday.

OpenAI said in March it was clocking $2 billion in monthly revenue, and Anthropic said last month that it had achieved an annual revenue run rate of $47 billion. Neither has disclosed GAAP financials so far. Anthropic’s expenditure and losses are unknown, but the Claude developer said it would report an operating profit of $559 million in the June quarter.

In March, OpenAI raised $122 billion in a funding round at a valuation of $730 billion, excluding the new investment. Its post-money valuation came out to be $852 billion, trailing Anthropic’s $965 billion valuation.

Last week, Elon Musk’s SpaceX (which includes Musk’s AI business, xAI) listed its shares on Nasdaq in a record-shattering IPO that raised $75 billion. SpaceX's revenue jumped 33% to $18.67 billion in 2025, but the company swung to a net loss of $4.94 billion from a profit of $791 million, according to its IPO prospectus.
Goldman has estimated ​that ⁠SpaceX's revenue would exceed $470 billion in 2030, while Morgan Stanley projected it would reach nearly $330 ⁠billion.

Last week, OpenAI said it had confidentially filed its IPO paperwork with the securities regulator, joining rival Anthropic in a push toward a ​stock market listing. It did not disclose the size or terms of the offering and said a timeline has not yet been determined.
Reuters and other outlets previously reported that the AI giant could target a valuation of up to $1 trillion in a stock market debut as early as September.
The FT reported, citing a source, that OpenAI’s high loss figure was largely due to its restructuring into a for-profit corporation, which was completed last October.
The majority of the increase in net loss last year was due to non-cash accounting charges tied to the company’s prior structure rather than its underlying operations, according to the report.

Before OpenAI’s switch, investors in the company received convertible interest rights rather than conventional equity. Under U.S. accounting rules, those interests were treated as liabilities and periodically revalued as the company’s valuation increased.

As OpenAI’s value rose, the increased value of those investor rights resulted in a roughly $30 billion charge, according to the FT source. The charge is not expected to recur following the restructuring, they said. Excluding restructuring charges and other non-cash items, the company’s loss was $8 billion.
According to Nasdaq Private Market, OpenAI’s valuation was last at $833.7 billion.

paragraphs: / Moonshot Nears $30 Billion Valuation After Kimi K3 Release

Moonshot, a Chinese artificial intelligence startup behind the Kimi chatbot, has returned to the center of the global AI race after releasing Kimi K3, a 2.8 trillion-parameter model that attracted intense attention at the World AI Conference. Developers and users crowded the company's exhibition area as interest shifted away from the larger booths of Alibaba Group Holding BABA , a Chinese technology and commerce company, and Tencent Holdings (TCEHY), a Chinese technology company whose Yuanbao platform previously integrated DeepSeek's R1 model. Artificial Analysis ranked Kimi K3 behind only Anthropic, the developer of Claude, and OpenAI, the developer of ChatGPT, in overall capability. Elon Musk described the model as impressive, while OpenAI strategy chief Dean Ball said its open-weight release could push the technology industry closer to what he called full AI communism. The response suggests that Chinese AI developers may be narrowing the performance gap with leading U.S. companies faster than many observers had expected.

Investor interest has accelerated alongside Moonshot's technical progress. The startup is finalizing a funding round that would value it at more than $30 billion and is considering a Hong Kong public listing in as soon as six months. Moonshot's valuation had already increased from $4.3 billion in December to $20 billion within five months, supported by investors including IDG Capital, Alibaba, Meituan, a Chinese food-delivery and local-services company, and several major Chinese state funds. Following the Kimi K3 release, Moonshot's daily sales rose by at least six times, forcing the company to temporarily stop accepting new subscriptions because of limited computing capacity. Investors may view the surge in demand, higher private-market valuation and potential listing as signs of growing commercial momentum, although the subscription freeze also suggests that access to computing resources could constrain near-term expansion.

Moonshot's resurgence follows a difficult period after DeepSeek, a Chinese artificial intelligence developer, released its R1 model in early 2025 on the same day Moonshot introduced its closed-source K1.5 model. DeepSeek's rapid rise caused users to leave Kimi and prompted founder Yang Zhilin to stop marketing the consumer chatbot, shift attention toward enterprise and software-development customers, and open-source Moonshot's next flagship model. The company later released the one-trillion-parameter K2 model, followed by K2.5 in January 2026 and an agent swarm designed to automate enterprise workflows. These products helped lift annual recurring revenue above $100 million in March 2026, $200 million in April and $300 million in June, according to people familiar with the figures. For investors, Moonshot's recovery could strengthen interest in China's open-source AI sector, while its rapid valuation growth and rising revenue expectations may intensify comparisons with DeepSeek and other Chinese developers competing with OpenAI and Anthropic.

Elon Musk described the model as impressive, while OpenAI strategy chief Dean Ball said its open-weight release could push the technology industry closer to what he called full AI communism. The response suggests that Chinese AI developers may be narrowing the performance gap with leading U.S. companies faster than many observers had expected.

Investor interest has accelerated alongside Moonshot's technical progress. The startup is finalizing a funding round that would value it at more than $30 billion and is considering a Hong Kong public listing in as soon as six months. Moonshot's valuation had already increased from $4.3 billion in December to $20 billion within five months, supported by investors including IDG Capital, Alibaba, Meituan, a Chinese food-delivery and local-services company, and several major Chinese state funds. Following the Kimi K3 release, Moonshot's daily sales rose by at least six times, forcing the company to temporarily stop accepting new subscriptions because of limited computing capacity. Investors may view the surge in demand, higher private-market valuation and potential listing as signs of growing commercial momentum, although the subscription freeze also suggests that access to computing resources could constrain near-term expansion.

Moonshot's resurgence follows a difficult period after DeepSeek, a Chinese artificial intelligence developer, released its R1 model in early 2025 on the same day Moonshot introduced its closed-source K1.5 model. DeepSeek's rapid rise caused users to leave Kimi and prompted founder Yang Zhilin to stop marketing the consumer chatbot, shift attention toward enterprise and software-development customers, and open-source Moonshot's next flagship model. The company later released the one-trillion-parameter K2 model, followed by K2.5 in January 2026 and an agent swarm designed to automate enterprise workflows. These products helped lift annual recurring revenue above $100 million in March 2026, $200 million in April and $300 million in June, according to people familiar with the figures. For investors, Moonshot's recovery could strengthen interest in China's open-source AI sector, while its rapid valuation growth and rising revenue expectations may intensify comparisons with DeepSeek and other Chinese developers competing with OpenAI and Anthropic.

paragraphs: OpenAI has unveiled an unexpected addition to its merchandise lineup—a ChatGPT-branded basketball priced at $70. The product is part of the company’s new “Pause. Play. Prompt.”…

Made entirely of durable rubber, the basketball is designed for both indoor and outdoor play. Alongside the basketball, OpenAI has also introduced a collection of branded merchandise, including a mini keyboard and premium apparel featuring AI-inspired designs and motivational phrases.
The basketball is part of a broader merchandise collection celebrating the ChatGPT brand.
The product combines OpenAI’s technology-focused identity with a lifestyle-oriented marketing campaign.
The basketball is one of several branded products released by OpenAI.
The merchandise is aimed at users who want to engage with the brand beyond its AI products.
The new collection reflects OpenAI’s growing focus on building ChatGPT into a recognizable global consumer brand.
The campaign reinforces the message that innovation can extend beyond software into everyday experiences.
The merchandise collection blends technology branding with lifestyle products designed for ChatGPT users and fans.
Technology companies are increasingly investing in consumer merchandise to strengthen brand identity.
For OpenAI, the initiative reflects the growing mainstream appeal of ChatGPT as both a product and a global brand.
While branded merchandise can strengthen customer engagement, OpenAI may face several challenges.
Differentiating products in a competitive merchandise market.
Expanding lifestyle products without diluting the core brand.
The long-term success of the merchandise strategy will depend on consumer interest and continued growth of the ChatGPT ecosystem.

The launch of the ChatGPT basketball demonstrates OpenAI’s ambition to evolve ChatGPT into a broader consumer brand rather than solely an AI application. Through its “Pause. Play. Prompt.” campaign, the company is encouraging users to combine technology with real-world experiences, highlighting the importance of creativity and physical activity alongside digital productivity.

As ChatGPT’s global user base continues to grow, OpenAI may expand its merchandise portfolio with additional lifestyle products that strengthen community engagement and brand recognition. While the basketball itself is an unconventional offering, it reflects the company’s broader strategy of extending its presence beyond software and into everyday consumer experiences.

OpenAI’s branded merchandise initiative illustrates how AI companies are increasingly building consumer-facing brands that extend beyond their core technologies. As generative AI becomes more mainstream, companies are looking for new ways to connect with users through physical products, events, and lifestyle experiences.

sourceContent.headline: Anthropic's $1.5B joint venture Ode puts forward-deployed engineers inside enterprise clients to close the AI implementation gap
sourceContent.description: Ode with Anthropic launches as a $1.5B joint venture to embed forward-deployed engineers inside enterprises, backed by Blackstone and Goldman Sachs.
paragraphs: Ode, a $1.5 billion joint venture involving Anthropic and backed by major investors, embeds engineers directly within enterprise clients to enhance AI implementation. This approach aims to close the gap in AI deployment by positioning technical expertise closer to business needs. The collaboration involves significant financial backing from Blackstone, Goldman Sachs, and Hellman & Friedman.
This story was produced through MarketScale . See how Software & Technology teams put it to work with Executive Thought Leadership .
Ode is a $1.5 billion joint venture aiming to improve AI implementation in enterprises.
The initiative places engineers directly within client enterprises for effective AI deployment.
Major investors in the venture include Blackstone, Goldman Sachs, and Hellman & Friedman.
The implementation gap that a $1.5B bet is trying to close
Forward-deployed engineers: consulting with a different cost structure
What the JV structure signals for enterprise AI procurement

Anthropic's enterprise AI joint venture now has a name, a valuation, and a list of heavy-hitting backers. Ode with Anthropic launched in May 2026 at a $1.5 billion valuation, according to TechCrunch, with capital and strategic backing from Blackstone, Goldman Sachs, and Hellman & Friedman . The thesis is direct: the next major commercial category in AI is not building better models but getting enterprises to actually use them.

AI model capability has outpaced enterprise deployment for most of the past two years. Labs including Anthropic and OpenAI have each launched separate businesses specifically designed to bridge that gap, according to TechCrunch 's reporting on both ventures. Ode represents Anthropic's answer to a growing recognition that selling API access is not the same as delivering operational value.

The vehicle Anthropic chose is a joint venture structure rather than an internal professional services team. That decision keeps Ode legally and operationally distinct while still giving it privileged access to Anthropic's models, roadmap, and technical expertise. The financial backing from Blackstone and Goldman Sachs adds balance-sheet weight and enterprise distribution relationships that a pure AI startup would take years to build.
The biggest commercial opportunity in enterprise AI right now may not be on the model side at all, it's in the implementation layer that most software vendors have never prioritized.

Ode's operating model centers on forward-deployed engineers, a model Palantir popularized in the defense and intelligence sector before it became a template for commercial AI services. Ode embeds these engineers directly inside client organizations, where they build and configure AI workflows against live enterprise data and existing systems rather than handing off a product and walking away.

The venture is led by Chris Taylor and Eddie Siegel, who co-founded Fractional AI before bringing that experience to Ode, according to TechCrunch's Equity podcast. Their background in fractional AI staffing for enterprises gives the leadership team a practical foundation that distinguishes Ode from a consulting brand built on slide decks. The core question the model poses is whether a small team of deeply embedded engineers can deliver results at a scale and speed that traditional systems integrators cannot match.

For procurement and IT operations leaders, the Ode structure raises a specific evaluation question: is this a services engagement, a software contract, or something new? The answer matters for budgeting, vendor management, and internal resourcing. Ode sits closer to a managed services or embedded consultancy arrangement than a SaaS subscription, which means procurement teams should expect outcome-based or time-and-materials pricing frameworks rather than per-seat licensing.

The backing from Blackstone is notable for a different reason. Blackstone's portfolio spans real estate, financial services, and infrastructure, and the firm has been vocal about deploying AI across its own operating companies. Its involvement in Ode gives the venture a near-captive proving ground of large-scale enterprise clients in industries where AI workflows around asset management, underwriting, and operations are high value and highly complex.

Anthropic 's simultaneous move into implementation services, alongside a similar initiative from OpenAI, points to a structural shift in how foundation model companies plan to generate revenue beyond API consumption. Both labs appear to have concluded that the enterprises willing to pay the most for AI are also the ones most likely to need significant help deploying it, and that leaving that work to third-party integrators means ceding both revenue and strategic influence over how their models get used.

sourceContent.headline: The Early Scale: 72% of B2B Buyers Now Vet Vendors on ChatGPT as Anthropic Backs a $1.5B Bet on AI Implementation
sourceContent.description: 72% of B2B buyers now vet vendors on ChatGPT. Token costs are blocking enterprise AI at production scale. And Anthropic just backed a $1.5B bet that the real problem is implementation, not the technology itself.
paragraphs: The article highlights critical trends affecting B2B buyers and enterprise AI. A significant percentage of B2B buyers are now using ChatGPT to evaluate vendors, while high token costs are hindering the scalability of enterprise AI applications. Anthropic is heavily investing in resolving implementation challenges, suggesting the issues lie more in application rather than technology.
This story was produced through MarketScale . See how Business Services teams put it to work with Executive Thought Leadership .
High token costs are obstructing AI deployment on a large scale in enterprises.
Anthropic is investing $1.5 billion to address AI implementation challenges.
72% of B2B Buyers Use ChatGPT to Vet Vendors. Most Brands Don't Show Up.
Palo Alto CEO: Token Costs Must Fall 90% in Two Years for Enterprise AI to Scale
Anthropic and Blackstone's $1.5B Venture Ode Embeds Engineers Directly Inside Enterprise Clients
Teach me something: GEO: Generative Engine Optimization

Good morning. It's Tuesday, and the story of this week is already clear: AI is everywhere, but scaling it is the hard part. Token costs are too high, governance frameworks are too thin, and enterprise buyers are now researching vendors on ChatGPT before they ever visit your website. The gap between "we deployed AI" and "AI is working for us" is where most businesses are stuck right now. Let's close that gap, starting with your next five minutes.

Nearly three-quarters of B2B software buyers now use ChatGPT as part of their vendor evaluation process, according to new research cited by MarketScale. The problem: 51% of tech brands have zero AI citations in large language model outputs. If an enterprise buyer asks ChatGPT who the best vendor is in your category and your name doesn't appear, you're not in the deal.

The B2B angle: Audit your brand's LLM presence this week by querying ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini with the exact phrases your buyers use to find vendors in your category, then build a GEO content strategy to close the gap.

Nikesh Arora put a precise number on a problem every enterprise CIO already feels: AI inference costs are still too high to run at production scale. He says token prices need to drop 90% within two years for the economics to work. As evidence, Uber burned through its entire full-year AI budget by April. This isn't a niche concern for tech companies; it's a capital allocation problem for any business running AI workloads.

The B2B angle: Before expanding AI pilots to production, model out your per-token cost trajectory against projected usage volume and build a cost ceiling into your AI budget now, before you hit Uber's problem at a smaller scale.

Ode, a $1.5 billion joint venture backed by Blackstone, Goldman Sachs, Hellman & Friedman, and anchored by Anthropic, takes a forward-deployed engineering model into enterprise AI adoption. Instead of selling software and leaving clients to figure out implementation, Ode puts engineers physically inside client organizations to close the gap between AI deployment and AI that actually works. It's a direct acknowledgment that the implementation layer is where enterprise AI breaks down.

The B2B angle: If your AI initiatives are stalling in the pilot phase, evaluate whether you need embedded technical partnership rather than another software license, and use Ode's model as a benchmark when negotiating implementation support from any AI vendor.

Global M&A hit a record $2.8 trillion in H1 2026, up 48% year-on-year, with industrial manufacturing surging 28% as AI infrastructure, grid modernization, and defense reshape deal flow. If you're in manufacturing, industrials, or energy, your competitive landscape is being redrawn right now.

Kyndryl's 2026 People Readiness Report finds 57% of enterprises run AI in core processes, but only 23% of leaders say their workforce is fully prepared. Deployment is outrunning training, and that gap is where costly AI failures happen.

HubSpot's State of Ecosystems 2026 report projects the partner opportunity at $42 billion by 2030, driven by mid-market demand for AI operationalization help. Channel and solutions partners who build AI implementation practices now are positioned to capture a disproportionate share of that growth.

Before your next AI vendor renewal or expansion decision, pull actual token usage logs for the past 90 days, project them against full-year production volume, and set a written cost ceiling in your AI budget before you hit overage. Uber burned its entire full-year AI budget by April, and Palo Alto's Nikesh Arora says current token economics still don't support production-scale deployment for most enterprises.

Audit your AI adoption roadmap against Kyndryl's 57/23 gap and schedule a workforce readiness assessment before you greenlight any new AI deployment in a core process. Kyndryl's 2026 data shows enterprises are deploying AI far faster than they're preparing workers to use it, and that gap is exactly where costly failures and poor ROI compound.

Token costs must fall 90% within two years for enterprise AI to scale. , Nikesh Arora, CEO, Palo Alto Networks

It's a rare moment of executive candor about the economics of AI at scale. Most enterprise AI conversations still center on capability. Arora is centering the conversation on cost, which is the actual constraint that separates pilots from production.

GEO is the practice of structuring your content, authority signals, and data so that AI-powered search tools like ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google's AI Overviews surface your brand in their responses. Unlike traditional SEO, which targets crawlable web pages ranked by algorithms, GEO targets the training data, citation patterns, and source preferences that large language models use when generating answers. For B2B brands, this matters because buyers are now asking AI tools to recommend vendors, compare solutions, and summarize categories before they visit a single website. If your thought leadership , product pages, and PR placements aren't structured to be cited by LLMs, you don't exist in that part of the buyer journey.

sourceContent.headline: The Early Scale: 94% of B2B Buyers Fact-Check AI Research. Vendors Are Losing the Trust War.
sourceContent.description: 94% of B2B buyers are fact-checking AI research outputs. The buying cycle is collapsing before vendors see a lead. And a $1.5 billion joint venture just launched on the premise that the real AI problem was never the model — it was always the implementation. Here's what that means for your week.
paragraphs: A significant majority, 94%, of B2B buyers are fact-checking AI research outputs, casting doubt on vendor trustworthiness. The B2B buying cycle is affected as leads are lost before vendors even engage with prospects. A $1.5 billion joint venture aims to address the issues with AI by focusing on implementation rather than the models themselves.
This story was produced through MarketScale . See how Business Services teams put it to work with Executive Thought Leadership .
The B2B buying cycle often collapses before vendors capture a lead.
A $1.5 billion joint venture focuses on improving AI implementation.
94% of B2B Buyers Fact-Check AI Research. Vendors Are Losing the Trust War.
AI Is Collapsing the B2B Buying Cycle, Before You Ever See a Lead
Anthropic and Blackstone's $1.5B 'Ode' Bets the Real AI War Is About Implementation

The week is opening with a theme that keeps repeating: AI is everywhere, but trust and cost are the two things nobody has fully solved. Buyers are fact-checking every AI output. Enterprises are blowing past their AI budgets. And a $1.5 billion joint venture just launched on the premise that the model was never the hard part, implementation is. If you're selling into or buying from an AI-driven stack, that's your context for everything you'll read this morning.

TrustRadius's 2026 B2B Buying Disconnect Report reveals that buyers are using AI faster than ever to research vendors, but nearly all of them are independently verifying what it tells them. That means AI is accelerating the research phase while simultaneously making every unverified vendor claim a liability. The trust deficit is real, and most vendors are not moving fast enough to close it.
The B2B angle: Audit every public-facing claim about your product right now, if AI tools are citing it incorrectly or outdated, buyers are already catching the discrepancy and moving on.

A companion finding from the same research: AI tools now compress weeks of vendor research into hours, meaning enterprise procurement teams are shortlisting, or eliminating, suppliers long before a sales rep ever gets a call. By the time a lead appears in your CRM, the decision may already be 80% made. The funnel is not just shorter; its top is now invisible to vendors.
The B2B angle: Your content strategy, G2 profile, and third-party reviews need to function as autonomous sales reps, because in many deals, they already are.

Anthropic and Blackstone launched Ode, a $1.5 billion joint venture that embeds elite engineers directly inside enterprise clients. The signal is loud: choosing the right model is table stakes; the differentiation is in the people and processes that make it actually work inside a real organization. For enterprises still stalled in AI pilot purgatory, this is a direct challenge to figure out the implementation layer.
The B2B angle: If your AI initiative is model-shopping rather than implementation-planning, you are working on the wrong problem, Ode's entire premise is that the gap is execution, not technology.

60% of agentic AI costs go to response refinement, and McKinsey finds 93% of enterprises are already over their AI budgets. If your team greenlit agentic deployments without mapping the iterative cost structure, the invoice is coming.

Global M&A hit $2.8 trillion in H1 2026, with mega-deals above $10 billion now accounting for nearly 50% of all deal volume, an all-time record. AI infrastructure and grid modernization are concentrating capital at the top of the market, and industrial manufacturing is the leading vertical.

The largest Cyclospora outbreak in U.S. history has hit nine states with 1,947 confirmed cases, and recalled product was distributed across 27 states. For food and beverage operators, this is a live stress test of your traceability infrastructure, not a drill.

Run a 'buyer eyes' audit of your top three competitor comparison pages, your G2/TrustRadius profile, and your homepage claims, specifically looking for anything an AI research tool might surface incorrectly or that you cannot back with a verifiable third-party source. With 94% of B2B buyers fact-checking AI outputs, a single unsupported claim caught during AI-assisted research can kill a deal before your team knows it existed.

Run a 'buyer eyes' audit of your top three competitor comparison pages, your G2/TrustRadius profile, and your homepage claims, specifically looking for anything an AI research tool might surface incorrectly or that you cannot back with a verifiable third-party source. With 94% of B2B buyers fact-checking AI outputs, a single unsupported claim caught during AI-assisted research can kill a deal before your team knows it existed.

Map your agentic AI deployments to a line-item cost model that breaks out response refinement separately from inference costs before your next budget review. McKinsey's finding that 60% of agentic costs go to response refinement means most AI budget models are structurally wrong, surfacing this now is cheaper than explaining overruns later.

Brief your demand-gen team that top-of-funnel content must now be optimized for AI retrieval, structured data, clear product specs, third-party citations, and updated review platforms, not just SEO rankings. The AI-collapsed buying cycle means procurement teams are building shortlists through AI tools before a sales rep is ever involved, so your discoverability in those tools is now a revenue variable.

Model selection is only one ingredient in AI transformation. The enterprises that win will be those that nail the implementation layer. , Ode with Anthropic Launch Announcement, Joint Venture Launch Statement, Ode / Anthropic / Blackstone

A $1.5 billion bet that the hard part of enterprise AI is not the model, it is the execution, is the most honest thing anyone in the industry has said publicly in months. Every CIO still running pilots should read it twice.

In agentic AI systems, 'response refinement' refers to the computational cycles an AI spends iterating on its own output, checking, correcting, and improving answers before returning them. Unlike a simple query-response model, agentic systems loop back on themselves multiple times per task, and each loop consumes tokens and compute. McKinsey found this single cost category consumes 60% of total agentic AI operating costs. Most enterprise AI budget models were built around inference cost, the price of asking a question once, and were never designed to account for this iterative overhead. That is why 93% of enterprises deploying agentic AI are already over budget.

The global ammonia market size is projected to grow from 197.35 million tons in 2026 to 216.72 million tons by 2031 . Agriculture remains the largest end-user, while power generation is expected to record the fastest growth among applications. Asia-Pacific continues to lead both production and consumption, supported by large agricultural demand and expanding industrial activities. Liquid ammonia remains the dominant product type, and growing interest in low-carbon ammonia for energy and shipping applications is influencing future industry investments.

Current Ammonia industry indicates that producers are investing in lower-carbon production methods while end users explore ammonia as a hydrogen carrier and an alternative fuel in selected energy applications. At the same time, established infrastructure for liquid ammonia transportation continues to support global trade. These factors are shaping the Ammonia Industry without changing its core role as a critical raw material for fertilizer production. The combination of established demand and emerging industrial applications supports the long-term Ammonia Market Forecast presented in the report.

Liquid ammonia accounted for 91.28% of the global ammonia market volume in 2025 due to its well-established storage, transportation, and distribution infrastructure. It remains the preferred form for large-scale industrial applications, particularly in fertilizer production and chemical manufacturing. Existing logistics networks and widespread handling facilities continue to support its dominant position across major producing and consuming regions.

Gas ammonia is projected to register the fastest growth, expanding at a CAGR of 4.18% during the forecast period. Rising demand from industrial refrigeration, emissions control systems, and emerging energy applications is supporting this growth. Increasing interest in ammonia as a hydrogen carrier and clean fuel is also encouraging investments in gas-based handling and distribution infrastructure.
Asia-Pacific Led the Ammonia Market and Will Remain the Fastest-Growing Region:

Asia-Pacific held 39.16% of the global ammonia market share in 2025 and is expected to remain both the largest and fastest-growing regional market through 2031. Strong fertilizer demand, expanding industrial activity, and ongoing investments in ammonia production capacity across China, India, and Southeast Asia continue to support regional growth. Government initiatives focused on energy transition and low-carbon ammonia projects are further strengthening the region's market position.

sourceContent.headline: AI is deployed in 57% of enterprises, but only 11% have hit their top two goals
sourceContent.description: Kyndryl's 2026 study of 1,100 leaders finds 57% have deployed AI broadly, yet only 11% have hit both top goals and workforce readiness is falling.
paragraphs: The deployment of AI technology in enterprises has reached 57%, yet only 11% have achieved their primary objectives according to Kyndryl's 2026 People Readiness Report. This increase in AI adoption is contrasted by a decline in workforce confidence and the attainment of business goals.
This story was produced through MarketScale . See how Software & Technology teams put it to work with Executive Thought Leadership .
Only 11% of enterprises have achieved their top two AI-related goals.
There is a decline in workforce confidence despite increased AI adoption.

Fifty-seven percent of enterprises now have AI embedded in core business processes or deployed broadly across their organizations, up from 35% just one year ago. That is the headline figure from Kyndryl 's second annual People Readiness Report, published June 25, 2026, which surveyed 1,100 senior business and technology leaders across eight countries. The problem is what sits on the other side of that deployment number.

Only 32% of those organizations have achieved at least one of their top two AI objectives. A mere 11% have hit both. Deployment is running far ahead of outcomes, and the data points to a consistent culprit: the workforce side of the equation is being systematically underinvested.

Worldwide AI spending is forecast to reach $2.52 trillion in 2026, a 44% year-over-year increase, according to Gartner research cited in Kyndryl's report. The money is going into tools and infrastructure. Human enablement is not keeping pace.

Kyndryl's findings make that gap concrete. Only 23% of business leaders now believe their workforce is fully prepared for AI, a six-point drop from 2025. Nearly four in five respondents agreed that the pace of AI development will outstrip their organization's workforce, governance, and operating models. Confidence is falling precisely when it should be growing.

The picture is starker at the individual employee level. The Achievers Workforce Institute 's seventh annual State of Recognition Report, cited by MarketScale, found that just 19% of workers feel confident using AI tools, and only 18% feel supported in adapting to them. In a typical enterprise, more than 80% of the workforce lacks either the confidence or the clarity to integrate AI into daily work, even as leadership accelerates deployment.
Deployment is outrunning outcomes because most organizations are buying AI capability while deferring the harder work of building AI readiness.

Kyndryl's report isolates a cohort it calls Pacesetters: roughly 9% of respondents that are generating measurable AI returns. These organizations share three operational behaviors. They redesign roles around AI rather than layering AI onto existing job structures. They implement structured change management so employees understand the new operating model and have guardrails in place. And they build workforce readiness deliberately, treating it as a foundational investment rather than an afterthought.

The performance differential is concrete and significant. According to Kyndryl, Pacesetters are 1.5 times more likely to achieve AI-related revenue growth and 1.6 times more likely to report improved innovation in products and services compared to peers. They are also roughly twice as likely to have fully implemented AI governance across every dimension measured in the study.

The broader organizational picture shows how much ground most companies still need to cover. While 61% have redesigned roles to support AI adoption and 24% are creating new AI-focused management positions, only one-third have fully implemented employee training programs focused on working alongside AI tools. Another third have clear policies defining which decisions AI can and cannot make, and just 27% are operating a registry and monitoring capability for their AI systems, per the Kyndryl report.

The governance shortfall is becoming a near-term operational problem, not a future concern. Kyndryl's data shows 81% of organizations expect AI agents to make impactful business decisions within the next year. Only 25% completely trust AI systems operating without human oversight today. That trust gap is not just cultural; for operations, finance, and supply chain teams deploying agentic AI, it is a live risk in any workflow where automated decisions carry downstream consequences.

Kim Basile, CIO at Kyndryl, noted in the report's release that organizations investing in their people, through rethinking roles, dedicating resources to upskilling, and guiding employees through change, are achieving positive outcomes at a much higher rate. Mark Paulek, Kyndryl's Chief Human Resources Officer, added that the leaders pulling ahead are aligning skills, roles, and decision-making with how work is actually changing, and that when employees understand their role in the new system, trust and performance scale together.

The skills pipeline is tightening as well. Half of leaders surveyed, 52%, say it has become more challenging to find employees with the right skills to advance their AI strategy, according to the Kyndryl report. That figure points toward a procurement and talent implication that goes beyond training budgets: organizations that have not built internal AI fluency now face both a vendor dependency risk and a longer runway to ROI than their Pacesetter peers.

Audit your training coverage before your next deployment cycle: with only one-third of enterprises reporting fully implemented AI training programs, gaps in workforce enablement are the most common reason deployment fails to translate into outcomes.

Treat governance as an enabler of trust, not a compliance checkbox: Kyndryl's data shows organizations with stronger governance report higher workforce trust in AI strategy, and high-trust organizations are significantly more likely to report transformative outcomes.

Accenture (ACN) has put fresh focus on its stock by lifting its fiscal 2026 share repurchase authorization to US$7.5b and appointing Pradeep Prabhala to lead its India Market Unit.

sourceContent.headline: IT Services Market Size To Exceed $3.35 Trillion By 2035
sourceContent.description: IT Services Market is driven by enterprise digital transformation, AI-driven service delivery, cloud adoption, and managed cybersecurity solutions.
paragraphs: The global IT Services Market is entering a new phase of expansion as organizations across industries modernize technology ecosystems to improve operational efficiency, strengthen cyber resilience, and accelerate digital innovation. “According to a recent study by SNS Insider, the IT Services Market size valued at USD 1.50 trillion in 2025, is anticipated to grow to USD 3.35 trillion by 2035, registering a CAGR of 8.35% over the 2026–2035 forecast period.”

With more companies turning towards the cloud, enterprise software, artificial intelligence, and connected infrastructure, the demand for managed and professional IT services is growing. Organizations are looking for technology partners that will be able to offer them large-scale infrastructure management, application modernization, cybersecurity services, and ongoing operational support, while at the same time, making technology solutions easy and simple for them.

The fast pace of changes in the automation world is also changing the way IT services are provided. Intelligent monitoring, predictive maintenance, automated processes, and analytics are improving services and making it possible for service providers to maximize efficiency and create better value for their enterprise customers.
To Get Detailed Insights on the IT Services Market – Request a Sample Report
Enterprise Modernization and AI Adoption Create Significant Growth Opportunities

Organizations are heavily investing in digital transformation programs that require experienced IT partners who can combine cloud computing , AI platforms, data management, and enterprise software into one technology landscape. With the modernizing projects becoming more complicated, the demand for outsourcing specialized technology services has risen for businesses from different industries.

The increasing shift to subscription-based and managed service approaches has opened up opportunities for the generation of regular revenues in the IT ecosystem. Companies more often opt for flexible service contracts that offer continuous technological upgrades, reasonable operational costs, and flexible provision of the services with no need to employ large IT teams.

At the same time, cyber security continues to develop as one of the most actively-developing branches of investments. The increase in cyber threats, expanding check requirements, and growing digital assets push organizations to improve security practices with the help of managed security services, risk assessment, compliance tracking, and advanced threat detection services.
Key Market Insights Highlight Changing Enterprise Technology Priorities

Based on type, Operations & Maintenance accounted for approximately 54.1% of market revenue in 2025 due to the continuous need for infrastructure support, application maintenance, and performance optimization. Design & Implementation is projected to record the fastest expansion through 2035 as enterprises accelerate digital transformation projects and cloud migration initiatives.

By approach, Proactive IT Services represented around 58.5% of total revenue in 2025 owing to growing adoption of preventive monitoring and predictive maintenance strategies. Reactive IT Services is expected to register the highest growth during the forecast period as organizations continue requiring specialized incident response and technical recovery services.

In terms of application, Systems & Network Management held nearly 47.8% market share in 2025 as businesses prioritize uninterrupted IT operations across hybrid infrastructure environments. Security & Compliance Management is anticipated to witness the strongest growth through 2035 due to increasing cybersecurity investments and expanding regulatory obligations. Among end users, enterprises remained the leading customer segment because of large-scale technology deployments, while government organizations continue increasing investments in digital modernization programs.
AI-Powered Service Delivery Reshapes Competitive Landscape

More and more technology service providers are using AI within their service management platforms to help them automate processes, improve incident resolution, and increase operational transparency. AI-based analytics are allowing businesses to identify problems with their infrastructure sooner, which means better levels of system availability and reduced downtimes.

All the above factors are driving demand for hybrid cloud management, IT automation, smart network operations, and data-driven business services, as companies are aiming to expand their consulting capabilities in addition to their managed services offering. Continuous investment in cloud engineering, implementation of AI, cybersecurity, and digital workplaces will ensure long-term competitiveness in the industry.
North America Held 36.5% of the IT Services Market Share in 2025; Asia Pacific Projected to Register the Fastest CAGR Through 2035

In 2025, the North American market is projected to account for around 36.5% of the global market revenue, largely due to high enterprise technology spending and cloud adoption, managed services, and cybersecurity investments across sectors. Thus, the U.S. is one of the major drivers of the regional demand with the implementation of digital transformation programs in state and commercial sectors.

The highest growth is anticipated for the Asia Pacific region in the period from the year 2021-2028. The expansion of enterprise digitalization, development of cloud infrastructure, increasing AI adoption, and great technology spending by countries, such as India, China, Japan, and Southeast Asia will be the factors of the rapid growth of this region.

sourceContent.headline: Graphic Processing Unit (GPU) Market Size to Hit USD 1712.56 Bn by 2035
sourceContent.description: The global graphic processing unit (GPU) market size is expected to be hit around USD 1712.56 billion by 2035 from USD 101.54 billion in 2025, with a significant CAGR of 32.62%.
paragraphs: The global graphic processing unit (GPU) market is projected to grow from USD 101.54 billion in 2025 to USD 1,712.56 billion by 2035, registering a remarkable CAGR of 32.62%. Growth is driven by the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, cloud computing, data centers, gaming, Internet of Things (IoT), autonomous vehicles, and immersive AR/VR applications, alongside continuous advancements in GPU architectures that enhance computing performance and energy efficiency.

The global graphic processing unit (GPU) market size is calculated at USD 101.54 billion in 2025 and is predicted to increase from USD 136.06 billion in 2026 to approximately USD 1712.56 billion by 2035, expanding at a CAGR of 32.62% from 2026 to 2035. The demand for graphic processing unit (GPU) market is expected to rise during the forecast period with growing sales of portable electronics, popularity of Internet of Things (IoT) and wearables.
Asia Pacific led the market with the biggest market share of 32% in 2025.
By device, the smartphone segment has held the largest market share in 2025.
By type, the hybrid GPUs segment is expected to expand at the fastest CAGR over the projected period.
By type, the integrated segment had the largest market share in 2025.
The wide adoption of AI, AR, and VR technologies pushes the demand for GPUs in industries ranging from gaming to corporate applications.
Increasing sales of gaming laptops and PCs, along with immersive entertainment experiences, support the consumer GPU segment.

Wearable and portable electronics markets and IoT integration parity improve the acceptance of GPUs. Developments in GPU architectures help increase efficiency and performance while enabling real-time rendering.
Increasing implementation of GPUs in data centers, cloud computing , and high-end tasks also opens bigger market opportunities.
Role of Graphic Processing Unit (GPU) for Artificial Intelligence (AI)

One of the prominent trends for the graphics processing unit market includes growing shifts towards the development of energy-efficient designs for GPUs offering high performance with low power consumption. This trend is popular and more in-demand for data centers where usage of energy should be limited to achieve carbon neutrality or low low-carbon emission goal to comply with environmental regulations set by authorities.

The growing demand for autonomous vehicles is further expanding the production of highly efficient GPUs that enable cars capable of process huge amounts of data in real-time. GPUs are essential to enable self-driving systems. Many autonomous companies are engaging to invest in technologies like GPUs, which are emerging as a key trend for the market. For instance, companies like Waymo and Tesla are using powerful GPUs for their self-driving car.

Expansion of cloud-based GPU systems is another notable trend for the market, which is adopted by many leading marketers like Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud that offer GPU-based instances that help in high-performance computing outputs for several industries using technologies like AI, big data analytics, and gaming.

The increasing use of AI and machine learning is again expanding the adoption of graphics processing units. GPUs are helpful for accelerating AI algorithms, making them crucial for various markets like finance, healthcare, and cybersecurity .
Why are integrated GPUs experiencing increased demand in the smartphone segment?

The smartphone devices emerged as the dominating segment in the global GPU market for the year 2025 and expected to maintain the same trend over the forecast period. The growth of the segment is attributed to the significant demand of durable as well as less power consuming GPU that foster the growth of integrated GPUs in the smartphone segment. In addition, smartphone manufacturers develop products that support AR and VR that projected to offer significant opportunity for the smartphone GPU market. Moreover, increasing adoption of smartphones for gaming purpose has surged the demand for high-end computing systems that can serve graphics-intensive gaming applications.

On the other hand, the other segment anticipated to witness the highest growth rate during upcoming years because of rising demand for small sized and efficient GPUs in other devices for example medical equipment that can potentially spur the graphic computing quality and speed.

Role of Graphic Processing Unit (GPU) for Artificial Intelligence (AI)

This trend is popular and more in-demand for data centers where usage of energy should be limited to achieve carbon neutrality or low low-carbon emission goal to comply with environmental regulations set by authorities.

The growing demand for autonomous vehicles is further expanding the production of highly efficient GPUs that enable cars capable of process huge amounts of data in real-time. GPUs are essential to enable self-driving systems. Many autonomous companies are engaging to invest in technologies like GPUs, which are emerging as a key trend for the market. For instance, companies like Waymo and Tesla are using powerful GPUs for their self-driving car.

Expansion of cloud-based GPU systems is another notable trend for the market, which is adopted by many leading marketers like Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud that offer GPU-based instances that help in high-performance computing outputs for several industries using technologies like AI, big data analytics, and gaming.

The increasing use of AI and machine learning is again expanding the adoption of graphics processing units. GPUs are helpful for accelerating AI algorithms, making them crucial for various markets like finance, healthcare, and cybersecurity .

Why are integrated GPUs experiencing increased demand in the smartphone segment?

The smartphone devices emerged as the dominating segment in the global GPU market for the year 2025 and expected to maintain the same trend over the forecast period. In addition, smartphone manufacturers develop products that support AR and VR that projected to offer significant opportunity for the smartphone GPU market. Moreover, increasing adoption of smartphones for gaming purpose has surged the demand for high-end computing systems that can serve graphics-intensive gaming applications.

On the other hand, the other segment anticipated to witness the highest growth rate during upcoming years because of rising demand for small sized and efficient GPUs in other devices for example medical equipment that can potentially spur the graphic computing quality and speed.

In what ways do hybrid GPUs combine the benefits of both dedicated and integrated GPUs?

The integrated segment led the GPU market by type with a prominent value share in 2025 and expected to retain its position during the forthcoming years because integrated GPUs find wide application in portable electronic devices that include tablets, smartphones, laptops, wearable's, and many others. In addition, the market witness significant research activities dedicated towards the development of integrated GPUs that are capable enough to aid high graphic processing in supercomputers, AI platforms, and VR systems.

Besides this, hybrid GPUs predicted to register the highest growth over the analysis period as hybrid processors have capabilities of both dedicated and integrated GPU that makes them a preferred choice for the software developers to improve the efficiency of graphics-intensive applications.

IT and Telecommunication segment dominated the market in 2025. The responsible IT departments are stimulating the use of tech-inspired excellence that expands the high-performance tech expertise in the market. IT services have been modified with smart, visualized intelligence that long supports the industrial needs suitable for the operational departments. The popular Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Google hyperscalers are expanding the demand in the market. This sharpens the data centers and smart tech space with more precision.

The media and entertainment segment is expected to grow during the forecast period due to rising animation and visualized modernization. The computing GPU solution in this industry marks great quality for the production house, emerging as a graphic hub for the best-in-class series or movies. The visual effects and 3D animation spur massive revenue in the market. The creators are receiving the benefit of the GPUs that help to deliver remarkable 3D scenes. The blockbuster VFX and AI merge promotes content and films with excitement, highlighting impeccable graphics.

What is the Asia Pacific Graphic Processing Unit (GPU) Market Size?

The Asia Pacific graphic processing unit (GPU) market size is calculated at USD 32.49 billion in 2025 and is predicted to worth around USD 43.54 billion by 2026, to approximately USD 548 billion by 2035, at a CAGR of 32.65% from 2026 to 2035

The Asia-Pacific dominated the global graphics processing unit market in the year 2025 and is projected to retain its dominant position during the forecast period. The growth of the region is attributed to the significant investment from the government to generate high graphic computing systems used for defense & intelligence coupled with the rising incorporation of IoT systems that demand efficient graphic computing systems. Furthermore, rising penetration of the internet and smartphones in the region accounted as the other most important factors escalating the demand for graphic processing units over the forecast timeframe.

Advanced Technology Adoption Drives North American GPU Market Growth

North America holds a significant revenue share in the graphic processing unit market. The growth of the region is attributed to the higher adoption of advanced technologies in countries like the U.S. and Canada. The presence of strong cloud infrastructure is also a major contributor in the region's growth where Microsoft Azure, AWS, Google Cloud have deployed vast GPU farms for cloud AI and data processing. The higher investments towards R&D has made them a popular spot for more innovative ideas to that can be helpful in defense contracts and many more.

The country is one of the world-leader in the tech industry due to the presence of leading GPU leaders like NVIDIA, Intel, AMD and many others. The cloud providers in the country have highly invested in GPU power for LLM training, AI integration and many more. The U.S. government has been highly focused on investing heay money on their national security and scientific research, which improves their spot in the graphic processing unit market. Additionally, the educational institutions in the country are highly focused on implementing AI and ML for various researches and experiments, which will drag more investments in the coming years. The rapid growth of the gaming industry in the country is expected to create more demand for GPUs in high performance PCs.

Europe's Status in the Graphic Processing Unit (GPU) Market

Europe's market is considered to be a significantly growing area, due to the favorable status of the manufacturing unit that polishes domestic fabrication in GPU production. The contribution of US-based tech leaders that support the regional market growth is expanding space for accessibility to diversified industries. This good business relationship elevates the recognition of GPUs into the popular sectors, flourishing the need for the same. The eco-friendly AI use is a complementary innovation that exceeds the expectations from the regional market for sustainable tech solutions, altering or adding value to the existing market trends.

Latin America's market is expected to grow at a notable CAGR in the foreseeable future. The hyperscalers' major role in the market runs the whole industrial game, seeking tech-associated power to scale up their respective business. The billions of funding to the high-tech infrastructure space is eventually uplifting the tech leaders' efforts, contributing to the countryside innovations. The smart partnerships with the hyperscalers bolster the GPU as a service base. The regional data center GPU expansion is a huge investment in market perfection.

sourceContent.headline: Steam AI Disclosure Hits 20% of Games as Rivals Skip [2026]
sourceContent.description: Steam's AI disclosure policy covers 1 in 5 new releases in 2026. Epic, PlayStation, Xbox and Nintendo still have no equivalent rule.
paragraphs: Valve spent two years building the video game industry’s most detailed rulebook for AI-generated content. On January 16, 2026, it rewrote large chunks of that rulebook, narrowing what developers must disclose and drawing a sharper line between tools used behind the scenes and content a player actually sees. More than five months later, the gap that rewrite exposed has only gotten wider. Steam now carries AI disclosure labels on roughly one in five new releases, according to tracking cited across multiple outlets that cover Valve’s policy. Epic Games Store, the PlayStation Store, the Xbox Store, and the Nintendo eShop still have no comparable public rule. Google Play applies disclosure only to a narrow set of “sensitive” categories. Apple’s App Store has none at all.
What Changed in Steam’s January 2026 AI Disclosure Rewrite
Steam vs. Epic vs. Consoles vs. Mobile: The Platform Divide
Market Impact: Disclosure Lands Amid Valve’s Own Antitrust Fight
The Sketchfab Contradiction Inside Epic’s Own Ecosystem
Historical Context: Platforms Have Written Content Rules Before

This is not a small technicality buried in developer paperwork. Steam’s AI disclosure system is quickly becoming the closest thing the game industry has to a real AI content law, and Valve wrote it alone. Steam controls an estimated 74% to 75% of PC digital game distribution by revenue. That scale turns any policy Valve adopts into a de facto industry standard, whether or not a single regulator ever steps in.
Add Tech Insider once in the Google app and our stories appear in your news suggestions.

Steam’s AI disclosure requirement is not new. Valve introduced it in January 2024 through the Steamworks Content Survey, the same intake form developers already used to flag mature content before a game reaches the store. The January 16, 2026 update, first reported by PC Gamer and confirmed by Game Developer , did not remove the requirement. It redrew the boundary of what counts.

Before the rewrite, developers faced real ambiguity over whether AI-assisted coding tools counted as “AI use” requiring disclosure. Valve’s clarified language now exempts internal workflow tools. A studio leaning on an AI coding assistant to speed up development does not need to say so on its store page. What still requires disclosure is anything a player actually sees or hears: AI-generated art, audio, dialogue, localization, or marketing material that ships inside the game or appears on its Steam page.

The distinction sounds simple on paper. In practice, it forced Valve to define two separate content buckets inside the Generative AI Content section of the survey, each carrying its own disclosure text and its own rules for what developers must describe.

Pre-generated AI content covers anything created during development that ships with the finished game: character art, voice lines, background music, or written dialogue produced with generative tools. Live-generated AI content covers material a game creates while it is actually running, such as dynamic NPC dialogue or procedurally voiced characters that respond to a player in real time. Valve requires developers shipping live-generated content to describe, in writing, the guardrails they have built to stop that output from crossing lines the platform won’t allow. One category gets zero exceptions: live AI-generated content that is also Adults Only sexual material is barred outright, with no appeal path written into the policy.

Steam’s approach to AI disclosure has moved in stages rather than arriving fully formed. Valve launched the original requirement in January 2024, at a moment when generative tools were still a marginal presence in most Steam submissions. Adoption then accelerated far faster than the policy’s authors likely expected. By the first half of 2025, close to 8,000 games had filed an AI disclosure on Steam, up from roughly 1,000 across all of 2024, an eightfold jump in about eighteen months. That growth curve is what pushed Valve back to the drafting table. Developers and reporters covering Steamworks documentation both flagged confusion about where “using AI” stopped and “shipping AI content” started, and the January 2026 clarification was Valve’s answer.

The practical effect since mid-January has been a narrower but more consistently enforced rule. Fewer studios now over-disclose out of caution, since internal tools are explicitly carved out, while the pool of games disclosing player-facing AI content has kept climbing through the first half of 2026.

Two numbers in that table matter more than the rest. The jump from roughly 1,000 disclosed games in 2024 to 8,000 by the first half of 2025 shows how fast generative tools moved from novelty to normal practice in PC game development. And the search-volume swing, tracked by DataForSEO and cited in this analysis, shows that public interest hasn’t cooled since. Search demand for Steam’s AI disclosure rules roughly doubled between May and June 2026 alone, evidence that Valve’s policy is still actively shaping how players and developers evaluate new releases.

Steam’s own record $11.1 billion in first-half 2026 revenue gives the disclosure numbers extra weight. A policy covering one in five new releases on a storefront moving that much money is not a niche compliance footnote. It is a rule touching a meaningful share of a market worth double-digit billions every six months.
Valve’s own language, reported by GameFromScratch , breaks the Generative AI Content section of the Steamworks Content Survey into a structure that looks roughly like this:

That last exemption is the one that changed the most in January. A team using a coding assistant to write boilerplate, debug a build, or speed up level design no longer has to mention it anywhere on the store page. A team using a generative model to produce the voice lines players hear, the background art they see, or the store screenshots they browse before buying still does.
